Solo Health offers several key medical benefits designed to protect members from both routine healthcare expenses and larger medical bills.

Here’s a closer look at what is included.

Solo Health covers eligible preventive healthcare services at 100%, with no deductible required.

This can be particularly helpful for self-employed individuals who want to stay on top of their health without paying the full cost of every preventive appointment. However, diagnostic tests or treatments performed during a preventive visit may be billed differently.

Solo Health covers primary care physicians and medical specialists. Members can access participating providers through the MultiPlan PHCS network, now associated with Claritev.

You generally don’t need a referral to see a specialist. For most non-preventive visits, you’ll pay the applicable cost until you meet your deductible. After you meet your deductible, the plan covers eligible medical services at 100%, subject to plan terms.

One of the most important reasons to have health coverage is protection against unexpected medical emergencies. A serious accident, hospitalization, or surgery can result in tens of thousands of dollars in medical bills.

According to the company, emergency services are processed as in-network regardless of which hospital provides the care.

Certain planned hospital admissions and surgeries require prior authorization.

Solo Health covers eligible mental health and substance use treatment. This can include outpatient therapy and other qualifying services. However, limits apply.

For example, Solo Health limits outpatient mental health therapy to 40 visits per covered individual each year. Some mental health treatments may also require prior authorization. If you regularly use mental health services, review these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health includes prescription benefits administered through FairosRx. Preventive medications in Tier 1 are covered at $0. For other covered medications, members generally pay the discounted cost until they meet their deductible.

Afterward, prescription copays apply based on the medication’s tier. Some specialty medications can still involve high out-of-pocket costs.

Solo Health also lists maternity and newborn care among its covered benefits. This can include eligible prenatal services, childbirth, and medical care for newborns.

However, anyone planning to start or expand a family should review the plan’s maternity provisions, eligibility requirements, and applicable exclusions before enrolling. Don’t assume every pregnancy-related service will automatically qualify for payment.

One of the biggest questions when considering any health coverage option is how much you’ll pay. Solo Health offers three plan designs, each with a different deductible.

The main difference between these plans is how much you must pay toward eligible medical expenses before the plan pays most covered costs at 100%.

All three plans offer the same core coverage and provider network. The deductible you select influences your monthly payment. Generally speaking, plans with lower deductibles cost more per month, while plans with higher deductibles cost less.

Your actual monthly cost depends on factors such as your age, location, household composition, and eligibility. Because pricing is individualized, the best way to determine your cost is to request a quote directly from Solo Health.

Let’s say you choose the Solo Health plan with a $5,000 individual deductible. You would generally pay the applicable cost of eligible non-preventive healthcare services until you’ve spent $5,000 toward your deductible.

After that, the plan pays 100% of eligible medical expenses for the remainder of the plan year. However, prescription copays and potential out-of-network charges can still apply.

This is why it’s important to understand the difference between your deductible and your total possible healthcare expenses.

Solo Health advertises its deductible as the out-of-pocket maximum for eligible medical care.

This structure can make medical expenses easier to plan for.

However, the advertised maximum may not cover every expense you could incur.

Prescription copays, excluded services, and charges above the plan’s out-of-network reimbursement amount may result in additional costs.

When comparing plans, consider both your monthly payments and what you could reasonably afford if you had a major medical event.

Solo Health uses a six-tier prescription drug structure. Here is the company’s published schedule for covered medications after meeting the deductible.

Tier 1 preventive medications are available without meeting the deductible. For most other covered prescriptions, these copays apply after the deductible is satisfied. The plan also restricts certain expensive medications.

For example, the plan may exclude non-specialty medications that exceed specified price thresholds. If you take prescription medications regularly, check the company’s formulary to confirm whether your medications are covered and what they might cost.

A Health Savings Account (HSA) can be a valuable tool for managing healthcare expenses. HSAs can offer tax advantages when you contribute, invest, and use the funds for qualified medical expenses.

According to Solo Health’s published FAQ, the V2500 and V5000 plan designs are HSA-eligible, while the V10000 plan is not currently listed as HSA-eligible. However, HSA eligibility depends on federal tax requirements, not simply a plan’s marketing designation.

Before contributing, confirm that your specific coverage qualifies as an HSA-compatible high-deductible health plan under current IRS rules. This matters because deductible amounts alone don’t establish HSA eligibility.

Customer experiences can provide valuable insight when evaluating a healthcare company. However, a company’s advertised benefits differ from what customers experience when submitting medical claims.

Solo Health publishes information about its coverage, member services, and claims administration. It also offers concierge assistance and an online member portal.

Solo Health offers several features that may appeal to certain self-employed individuals.

Many freelancers and small business owners don’t have access to employer-sponsored health insurance. Solo Health is specifically designed for people in this situation.

Its business-based structure gives qualifying entrepreneurs another option to consider when shopping for health coverage.

Three deductible levels let members choose a plan that fits their financial situation. Someone with a larger emergency fund might prefer a higher deductible to reduce monthly costs.

Another person might prefer paying more each month in exchange for a lower deductible. The key is choosing a plan that fits both your budget and your ability to handle unexpected medical expenses.

Solo Health provides access to the MultiPlan PHCS network, which includes participating providers across all 50 states.

This may be especially valuable for entrepreneurs who travel frequently or work in multiple locations. Members can also seek out-of-network care, although additional financial risks can apply.

Unlike limited-benefit programs, Solo Health advertises coverage for major medical expenses such as hospital stays, surgeries, and emergency care.

It also includes preventive care, prescription benefits, and mental health services. The company states that there are no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits.

Solo Health’s business-based structure may offer tax advantages for eligible business owners. The company states that monthly plan costs are generally deductible as a business expense.

However, the tax treatment depends on your business structure and individual circumstances. Consult a qualified tax professional before assuming your payments will qualify for a deduction.

Eligible preventive services are covered at 100% from the beginning of coverage. This feature helps people prioritize preventive care while managing overall medical expenses.

While Solo Health has appealing features, it also has important limitations.

Solo Health requires applicants to have an eligible business with an active EIN. Applicants must also complete a health questionnaire.

If you don’t meet the company’s participation requirements, you may not qualify for coverage. This makes Solo Health less accessible than ACA Marketplace coverage, which generally offers guaranteed issue during applicable enrollment periods.

A $10,000 deductible may be manageable for someone with substantial savings. However, it could create financial hardship for someone living paycheck to paycheck.

Before selecting a high-deductible plan, make sure you have enough savings to handle unexpected healthcare costs. The lowest monthly payment isn’t necessarily the best financial decision if it exposes you to expenses you cannot afford.

Solo Health uses reference-based pricing for out-of-network services. This means the plan may reimburse a benchmarked amount rather than the provider’s full billed charge.

If the provider charges more than the plan allows, you could be responsible for the difference. This is sometimes called balance billing.

Although Solo Health offers support services to help members navigate medical bills, that does not necessarily eliminate the risk of additional charges.

Solo Health’s enrollment process includes health-related eligibility questions. This differs from ACA-compliant individual health insurance.

If you have ongoing medical conditions or a complicated medical history, review the eligibility requirements carefully.

Accurate answers are essential, and the company states that incomplete or inaccurate information can result in denial of coverage.

Although Solo Health advertises no annual or lifetime dollar caps on covered medical benefits, certain services have visit limits.

For example, outpatient mental health therapy is generally limited to 40 visits annually per covered individual. Some treatments also require prior authorization. Read the complete plan documents so you understand these limitations before enrolling.

Solo Health’s self-funded model may be unfamiliar to people who have only purchased traditional insurance.

The arrangement involves a self-funded business health plan, third-party administration, and a medical reimbursement policy.

Because this structure differs from a standard individual insurance policy, it is worth reviewing the legal and financial responsibilities involved.

How does Solo Health compare with a conventional ACA Marketplace plan?

Traditional ACA Marketplace insurance offers important consumer protections, including guaranteed coverage of preexisting conditions and standardized requirements for essential health benefits.

Solo Health offers a different structure that may appeal to qualifying business owners. However, these products are not interchangeable. For someone with ongoing medical needs, ACA-compliant coverage may provide greater predictability around eligibility and consumer protections.

For an eligible entrepreneur, Solo Health may be worth comparing based on its benefits, provider access, and total annual costs.

Another useful comparison is Solo Health versus healthcare-sharing organizations such as Zion HealthShare. Although both may appeal to people exploring alternatives to conventional individual insurance, they work differently.

Solo Health offers a self-funded major medical plan established through an eligible business.

Its structure includes formal plan documents, medical claims administration, and a self-funded plan structure.

Zion HealthShare is a healthcare-sharing organization. Members contribute monthly amounts to share eligible medical expenses within the community.

Healthcare-sharing programs are not insurance, and they don’t guarantee payment of medical expenses the same way an insurance contract does.

The better option depends on your needs. Solo Health may be more appealing to business owners who want a structured major medical plan with a nationwide provider network.

Zion HealthShare may appeal to people who are comfortable with the healthcare-sharing model and its guidelines. Don’t choose either based on monthly costs alone. Consider the eligibility requirements, exclusions, payment structure, and your financial exposure if you experience a major medical event.

Solo Health may be worth considering for:

It may be particularly appealing to someone who wants to explore a business-based health plan rather than purchasing coverage through the individual insurance market.

If you have significant ongoing medical expenses, compare your options carefully.

If you’re interested in Solo Health, you can start the enrollment process online.

Make sure you have an eligible business with an active EIN. Review the company’s health eligibility requirements before proceeding.

Visit Solo Health’s website and enter the information requested. Your quote will depend on your individual circumstances.

Review the three available plan designs. Consider both the monthly cost and what you might have to pay if you need significant medical care.

Answer the required health questions accurately. Enrollment is subject to approval.

Before completing enrollment, carefully review the plan’s Summary Plan Description, exclusions, and payment terms.

Once approved and enrolled, you can access your plan information through the member portal.

Solo Health operates a business-based, self-funded major medical plan with a defined administrative structure. However, a documented plan structure does not independently verify financial strength, claims performance, or customer satisfaction.

Prospective members should review the legal documents and verify the applicable entities and regulatory disclosures.

Solo Health requires a health questionnaire to determine eligibility. Unlike ACA Marketplace plans, enrollment is not guaranteed regardless of medical history.

Ask the company how its eligibility rules and plan terms apply to your specific circumstances.

Yes. Solo Health allows eligible business owners to include qualifying family members.

The company publishes family aggregate deductibles equal to twice the individual deductible.

Possibly. Solo Health uses the MultiPlan PHCS network.

Verify that your doctor participates in and accepts your specific plan before enrolling. Out-of-network care may be available, but additional charges can apply.

Solo Health generally allows members to choose a different deductible at renewal.

Mid-year changes require approval and may affect the monthly cost.

They may be deductible depending on your business structure and tax situation.

Consult your tax professional for guidance.

Solo Health advertises access to participating providers in all 50 states.

However, nationwide provider access does not necessarily mean every applicant or business can enroll in every state.

Confirm availability and eligibility directly with the company.

Solo Health offers an interesting alternative for self-employed individuals seeking major medical coverage outside the traditional individual insurance market. Its biggest advantages include multiple deductible options, access to a nationwide PPO network, preventive care benefits, and coverage for significant medical expenses.

For qualifying entrepreneurs, the business-based structure may also provide financial and tax-planning opportunities. However, there are important trade-offs. Applicants must meet health eligibility requirements, higher deductibles can create substantial out-of-pocket costs, and out-of-network billing can become complicated.

I recommend comparing Solo Health with at least two other coverage options before deciding. Look beyond the monthly payment and calculate what you might spend over an entire year, including deductibles, prescription costs, and potential out-of-network expenses.

The goal isn’t simply to find the cheapest health plan. It’s to find coverage that protects your health and your finances when you need it most. Eligible self-employed business owners may want to explore Solo Health.

Disclaimer: This article is for informational purposes only and is not medical, legal, insurance, or tax advice. Solo Health is a self-funded major medical plan using a captive-based funding structure, not an ACA Marketplace individual insurance policy or healthcare-sharing ministry. Official plan documents govern coverage, eligibility, exclusions, and reimbursement. Verify all details with the provider before enrolling.

Breaking free from the traditional 9-5 is more achievable than ever with these 26 innovative income streams. Ready to redefine your concept of earning?

Are you trying to win the Mega Millions, but your numbers never seem to come up? It may be time to look for better ways to make money. Fortunately, you can earn extra cash without going and getting a “real job.”

What are the best ways to avoid sitting in a cubicle all day? Some money-making strategies require an upfront investment, while others let you earn money in your free time with the help of apps.

Read on to learn the best ways to earn cash without a regular 9-5 job, plus tips on how almost anyone can get started.

One of the easiest ways to earn money is by signing up to participate in market research studies. You won’t make much, a few dollars here and there, but you can create a free account and get started within minutes.

You’ll be paid in PayPal cash or gift cards for sharing your opinion and completing other tasks online.

E-Poll Market Research is one of the top companies to consider for this type of work. They make it easy to create an account and answer survey questions.

However, there are plenty of other options to consider, including:

While market research gigs won’t make you rich, it’s something you can do during your spare time.

If you have a book idea, turning your story into an eBook can help you earn passive income without a regular job. Kindle Direct Publishing can even help you format your book for Kindle, at which point you can market and sell your book to millions of potential readers who shop on Amazon.com.

How much can you earn writing eBooks? That depends on how many books you write, how much you sell them for, and how successful you are at marketing your book. Selling 20 books per month with a profit of $7 per book would net you $140 per month and $1,680 per year.

Meanwhile, selling 100 books per month at $7 per book would net you $700 per month and $8,400 per year. Need a little inspiration? Here’s an article that shows you how to make your first $1,000 selling eBooks.

You can earn a lot of money by starting a blog or niche website and monetizing it. I should know. I started Good Financial Cents more than a decade ago, and have earned millions of dollars through the monetization of this site since its earliest days.

How do you make money blogging? Earning real income with a website isn’t as easy as it looks, but there are plenty of monetization strategies you can try.

Here are the most common ways blogs make money:

If you’re curious about what it takes to earn money blogging, consider signing up for my Make 1K Challenge. It’s free and can help you earn your first $1,000 online with some of the blog monetization strategies I’ve already mentioned.

You could argue that freelance work is like a regular job, but working at home and on your terms is much different from traditional employment. The fact is, most freelancers are fully remote – they can work from anywhere in the world with a laptop and an internet connection.

Plus, they can hire and fire clients based on their personal needs and preferences, and their income potential is unlimited. According to ZipRecruiter, freelancers in the U.S. average $63.53 per hour.

Of course, you’ll need a marketable skill to find paid work as a freelancer. This could be freelance writing, design skills, marketing expertise, or something else.

You can use several websites to market your skills as a freelancer, including:

HealthyWage makes it possible to earn money while you lose weight. You won’t earn a ton of cash through the app, but you can earn a few dollars and use it to supplement other income you have.

The more weight you lose, the more money you can make. For example, the HealthyWage website claims some of their clients who lost more than 100 pounds managed to earn anywhere from $1,400 to $3,000.

However, the HW weight loss calculator shows potential earnings of $578 to $828 for people who only have 15 pounds to lose.

If you have a car you rarely use and want to earn some side income, you can consider renting it out with Turo, a ride-sharing platform that connects car owners with people who need a short-term rental. You can set your price, although you’ll have more success if you price your car competitively.

Nicer vehicles in high-demand areas can easily fetch rates that surpass $100 per day through this platform. Turo notes that in-demand cars rented out regularly can bring in anywhere from $10,000 to $20,000 per year in net profit.

Plus, almost anyone can rent out their car provided it meets the guidelines of the Turo platform. Your car must be 12 years old or newer with less than 130,000 miles. It must be worth less than $200,000 (no Lambo’s), and you must also meet Turo’s auto insurance requirements.

Do you have a spare bedroom in your home that you never use? Maybe you have a basement or garage apartment you could fix up and begin renting for a profit?

Either way, Airbnb lets you rent out rooms and other spaces in your home on any dates you prefer. You must let renters know they’re renting a room in a home vs. an entire apartment or house and provide as much additional detail as possible.

The amount you can earn will depend on where you live and the type of accommodation you can offer. However, expensive cities like Chicago, New York, and San Francisco have plenty of rooms for rent that go for well over $100 per night.

You may not have an entire room you can rent, but even if you have some storage space, Neighbor.com allows you to rent it out to others in need.

Common spaces rented through this platform include

The Neighbor.com platform makes it easy to advertise your unused space so that people nearby can inquire if they’re interested. Also, note that the platform offers insurance that can protect you if some of your client’s items are damaged or stolen while in your care.

How much can you make renting out extra space? It depends on how much space you have to rent and where it’s located. However, Neighbor.com shows a range of rental space options that cost anywhere from $20 to $100+ per month.

Investing in dividend stocks is one of the best ways to earn money without a regular job. Many early retirees find a way to live and pay bills based solely on the dividends they receive from various stocks.

But what exactly is a dividend stock? For the most part, they are regular stocks but with a track record of sharing their profits with investors through dividends.

Dividends can also be earned in exchange-traded funds (ETFs) or mutual funds, and they can be significant once you build up a large portfolio.

Since dividends are paid by profitable companies, they tend to be seen as less risky for investors. If you’re curious about what it takes to get started with this strategy, this post explains how to invest in dividend stocks.

Housesitting is an option if you’re somewhat mobile and can move from place to place. Generally, you can find house-sitting gigs through word of mouth, referrals, or online portals like Craigslist.org or Facebook Marketplace.

That said, not all house-sitting gigs are paid. Some offer the potential for exotic travel instead and free lodging for a week to several months.

Either way, a website called TrustedHousesitters is the best place to find house-sitting gigs. Some jobs posted are for house-sitting only, while others require house sitters to provide basic care for pets or plants.

If you have serious wanderlust and want to travel far and wide, this platform can help make it happen. Many gigs posted online are in countries like Australia, Ireland, France, and Switzerland.

If you love animals and want to earn money taking care of them, several platforms can help turn your dream into a reality.

For example, Rover.com lets you provide basic care for dogs or cats in your home, or you can pick up dog walking gigs. Another mobile app, called Wag!, lets you do more of the same.

You can set your rates for all types of work through these platforms, and your availability. While earnings vary by location and job, most people watch dogs and cats for anywhere from $40 to $100 per night.

Real estate investing may seem like a pipe dream if you hope to earn income without a job but hear me out. There are many ways to earn income through real estate without owning physical property or dealing with the hassles of being a landlord.

You can invest in real estate investment trusts (REITs) that let you build wealth over time. You can also use a platform called Fundrise to invest in real estate with a minimum investment of $10.

Fundrise lets you purchase eREITs, large investment funds that acquire, own, or operate multi-residential and commercial properties. The income you earn is entirely passive since it handles the work of finding income-producing properties and managing them.

While returns are never guaranteed, Fundrise investors have achieved very solid returns. Investors who use the platform earned an average return of 7.31% in 2020, followed by 22.99% in 2021, 1.50% in 2022 and -7.45% in 2023 (their first down year).

You can earn income on your spare change by investing it using Acorns. The roundup savings app syncs to your debit or credit card rounds up every purchase you make to the nearest dollar, and invests the difference. Once it’s set up, there’s no work on your part.

Most of the money is invested in ETFs and managed by the world’s top investment firms like Vanguard and BlackRock. While this app makes it easy to invest small amounts of money, it’s not free to use. Personal plans start at $3 per month, while a family plan costs just $5.

If you’re looking for some paid gigs that are relatively easy, consider setting up a profile on TaskRabbit, an online platform that lets you get paid for completing various tasks, such as:

Projects typically pay between $30 and $100, although some pay significantly more than that. TaskRabbit also lets you pick and choose the jobs you want to take on based on your availability so that you can work entirely on your schedule.

If you love taking photographs and have a knack for getting professional-looking images, you can use your skills and expertise to sell photos online.

Websites like Depositphotos and iStockPhoto pay photographers to supply them with stock photos they can sell to writers, publications, and various online platforms.

The best part about this side hustle is that you can get started with the equipment you already have. While you can use a professional camera if you want to, many smartphones take professional-quality photos.

Earning a bank bonus is another way to earn money without a regular job, but you’ll need an upfront investment to get started. Most bonus offers require you to deposit a specific amount of money and keep it in your account for up to 12 months.

You may also be required to set up direct deposit to earn a bank bonus, and other terms and conditions may apply.

Where can you find the best bank bonuses? While bonus offers constantly change, you can start by checking with banks like Chase, HSBC, Radius Bank, and Wells Fargo.

Flipping furniture requires some upfront legwork and potentially even some artistic talent, but you can earn a solid income with this strategy if you know what you’re doing.

Essentially, this side hustle requires you to shop at thrift stores, garage sales, and online platforms to find furniture that will ultimately sell for more than you paid.

From there, you can sell the furniture as-is or clean it up and paint it with the goal of fetching an even higher price.

You can make money driving for Uber or Lyft on your own time, picking and choosing the days and hours you want to work.

Not only is rideshare work one of the most flexible side hustles, but you can earn $20 per hour and more with tips.

If you are low on free time but still want to make money without a job, consider selling stuff you don’t need. An array of online platforms makes it a breeze, although some platforms work better for selling.

For example, you can use Poshmark to earn money selling used clothing and accessories, while used electronics tend to sell best on platforms like eBay.com, Decluttr, BuyBackWorld, and Gazelle.

If you have home decor, furniture, or workout equipment to sell, you’ll almost always do better unloading those items locally on Facebook Marketplace.

Starting a YouTube channel is another way to earn money without a job, but that doesn’t mean it’s not work. The fact is, that creating quality videos and building an audience takes a lot of creativity and time. Plus, not everyone who tries to build a YouTube channel will succeed.

That said, you can earn income without a regular job. I know because I have done it with my YouTube channel, Wealth Hacker.

How much you can earn on YouTube varies quite a bit, but it’s possible to earn thousands of dollars per month. If you’re curious about monetizing videos, my in-depth guide will show you how to make money on YouTube.

Donating plasma is a unique way to earn money without a job, although it’s not very glamorous. DonatingPlasma.org makes it easy to find plasma donation centers in your area, and you can earn as much as $100 for your first donation.

That said, subsequent plasma donations typically earn closer to $50. You’ll also be limited by the number of times you can donate plasma within a month. However, it’s possible to use this side gig to earn an extra $500 per month, which you can use to supplement your primary income.

If you are willing to complete various tasks that help regular workers do their jobs, consider becoming a crowd worker. This gig will have you finishing up to-do lists of jobs that don’t require specific technical skills.

For example, you may get paid to proofread documents, label images, update a resume, complete a form, or complete a data entry assignment.

Several platforms help you find crowd-working gigs, but the best ones include Microworkers and Clickworker.

If you want to do something simple that will get you moving, consider delivering groceries using apps like Instacart or Shipt. You get paid hourly, plus tips and all you have to do is head to the store, purchase groceries according to a list, and deliver them to people in your neighborhood.

The gig is extremely flexible, similar to driving for Uber or Lyft.

Another non-job gig lets you get paid to deliver packages for Amazon.com. You can do this through a platform called Amazon Flex, which promises its drivers anywhere from $18 to $25 per hour.

Unlike a regular Amazon job, Flex lets you pick the day and the hours you want to work. To get started, you need to create a free account, get approved, and start reserving blocks of time you want to deliver packages.

Finally, you can earn money by selling unwanted or unused gift cards in your possession. This hustle is made easy thanks to platforms like GiftDeals.com and CardCash.com.

You won’t get the total value of your gift cards, but you should get 90% or more of the gift card balance for each card you sell. While selling gift cards for less than their total value may not seem ideal, it’s better than not using them and getting nothing in return.

Finally, you can earn small amounts of money by signing up with the best online survey sites. Not only is this side hustle as easy as it gets, but you can participate and get paid during your spare time and even on your phone.

Other online survey sites to check out include the following:

With all this being said, you’ll want to keep in mind that most surveys only pay a few bucks and that some only pay you with gift cards, while others offer the option for PayPal transfers. Make sure you understand how each survey site works and how you get paid before you sign up.

There you have it, 26 ways to make money without a job. While many of the jobs on our list won’t replace your 9-5, they can be a great way to increase your income so you can pay off debt or break the cycle of living paycheck to paycheck.

Check out the video below if you’re looking for even more ways to make money.

#8524. My Unexpected Journey to Hormone Replacement (TRT)

As a man of Science, I’m supposed to hide my enthusiasm about this somewhat controversial subject, and instead direct you only to the peer-reviewed studies.

But man, I feel like I’ve stumbled upon the fountain of youth here. And the more I dig into the details and the hype and controversy surrounding the field of Hormone Replacement therapy, the more I need to share the word about it to my fellow middle-aged people (both men and women).

I’ve been interested in optimization and trying to get the most out of my body and mind since I was a little kid. I started vacuuming up all the training and nutrition books and magazines I could find while I was just a teenager, and that field still remains a favorite of mine over 30 years later. And if you’re a long-time reader here you’ve been reminded plenty of times of this interest, because health has always been the very heart of Mustachianism.

But a funny thing has been happening in the last ten years: even as I kept honing the healthy living habits and trying my best to improve, there seemed to be a force pulling me back almost as hard. So despite working a bit harder and smarter every year, I still felt myself riding a gradually declining tide of energy, motivation, and physical stamina.

“Perhaps this is just what it means to grow old”, I thought to myself,

Yet there was one thing that didn’t quite fit. Why was I having this decline in energy, when some of my older friends weren’t? And why was I still seeing people out there in their 50s, 60s and well beyond doing things that I felt too tired to do today?

One of these tireless friends is a guy named Kevin, who is the personification of the highly energetic successful middle-aged man. He’s a semi-retired serial entrepreneur (and extreme rock climber) who lives in Boulder.  And through an interesting twist of fate, in April of 2025 he invited me out for a hike right around the time I was doing all this wondering. And during this hike (and climb) he told me about his latest venture, a boutique men’s health company that specializes in helping men just like us get their youth back through the process of testosterone replacement therapy.

Long story short: his ideas planted a seed in my head, which led to a bunch of research and a growing interest in trying TRT myself. I had of course heard about the process, but for some reason never considered doing it until I heard Kevin’s enthusiasm: he had been on it for several years, and according to him it is a “night and day difference” in all the things you want in life: energy, focus, thinking speed, and of course physical health.

Another convenient twist of fate is that I happen to be dating an REI doctor – a Reproductive Endocrinologist and Infertility specialist who has two board certifications in exactly the relevant bodily systems that are affected by these hormones. And while she was initially skeptical that I needed more Testosterone (and in her practice she regularly sees the downsides of men taking the stuff too early in life and thus compromising their own fertility), she has followed along and helped me learn at each step of this process, eventually becoming fully in support of the program.

So I signed up as a test customer for Kevin’s new company, which is called Bolt Health. I worked with their doctor to get a baseline blood test and review my numbers compared to all the past tests I’ve collected, and as it turned out, my levels had been dropping consistently over the years, and the latest test was by far the lowest ever.

Even more telling, my age-related drop in Testosterone was correlating perfectly with my decline in energy and motivation:

The next step was a prescription for a tiny daily dose of supplemental T, which arrived at my house the next week along with instructions for how to use it. And so began the journey.

Now let’s jump forward seven months to the present day as I write this.

And wow, what a great year it has been! I only wish I had known and tried this a few years earlier, because I’m getting a lot more out of my life.

It’s not a night-and-day difference for me, but more like a 50% boost in overall youthfulness and energy. The biggest subjective change is that I just don’t have sucky tired days anymore, which was the main problem with my life before: wasting too much of my precious freedom due to not having the energy to enjoy it.

This is why I’ve become somewhat of an evangelist for hormone replacement therapy for people from about age 45 onwards. It won’t work for everyone – if your levels are already pretty high, you don’t get the same boost. Two of my male friends tried TRT and quit because they didn’t notice any benefit. But these same two guys already had plenty of energy to begin with, which is usually a sign that the body has what it needs.

It turns out I am very late to this party. Although Testosterone supplementation started out as a niche practice in the 1940s, from the 2010s onward it has been everywhere.

TRT is the reason you see every actor suddenly showing up buff overnight for their superhero roles and it’s also why so many of today’s CEOs don’t look anything like yesterday’s CEOs.

In many cases, it has gone too far with young men using it just to gain muscle for the beach or the football field, and questionable online providers (aka “Prescription Mills”) handing out prescriptions to anyone with a valid credit card – with profit as their sole motive. It became overhyped in certain pockets of Bro Culture, where every Bro eventually receives the advice “Bro! You need to get on the T!” from another Bro, and therefore does it. And some of this reputation surely contributed to my own skepticism.

But there’s a lot of valid science behind TRT, if you’re the right candidate and you take the right dosage. And because of that, I feel it is probably under-hyped in my own demographic, the Nerdy Tech Worker Semi Retired Dad contingent. And that’s why I’m writing this blog post, because there are a lot of us out there.

Many of us just tend to work with what we were given, and accept that aging means slowing down. And for those of us already enjoying an early retirement, we have the option of unlimited rest and recuperation time, so who really cares if we get tired a bit more often? After all, what better way to flex one’s wealth than with a decadent Tuesday Afternoon Nap while everyone else is stuck in the office?

While this seemingly healthy attitude has a lot of positive aspects, it can also mask a real problem which may be easily fixable. Because sometimes, the only thing that’s even better than an afternoon nap, is having the energy and motivation to go out for an afternoon hike, bike ride or adventure with friends. More energy is also pretty darned useful if you’re still raising kids or trying to do well in your career as a person over 45.

How it Actually Works (and What Happened to Me)

Distilling all of the fluffy discussion above into the simplest possible answer: TRT means using a tiny needle to inject a few drops of clear liquid just below the surface of your skin. And you do this by yourself at home, ideally once every morning.

Here’s one of the baby needles I use for my daily dose.The typical serving is less than one tenth of a milliliter, which is only a few drops.

And while the term “needle” sounds scary to some, this is very different from the monstrosities they use to draw blood from your veins. This one is so miniature that you don’t need special training to use it, and you usually don’t even feel it.

So I began doing this to myself on May 1st of this year, while keeping a daily journal of my results along the way. The results seemed to be almost immediate in all the promised areas, but I know how powerful the Placebo Effect can be so I kept my skeptic’s hat on to see what would happen in the long run.

I was seeing increased energy and motivation as well as lean weight gain through the whole spring and summer, but I remember the first truly shocking observation happened during a mountain vacation in July. I was part of a multi-family trip with lively adults, chaotic kids, early mornings, late nights with a few drinks, very intense high altitude sunshine and nonstop physical activities. It was just the type of situation that would drain my energy pretty quickly in the past.

But on day three I went out on a solo mountain bike ride to explore the area, and as I was climbing a long ascent with the blazing sun cooking me from every angle I just somehow kept having plenty of energy to keep climbing. Then I came down and joined the group for a few games of full-sun pickleball, biked back up the mountain to our cabin, and the story of unlimited energy went on from there.

“Hot Damn”, I thought to myself, “I don’t know whose youthful and tireless body I have inherited here but I’d sure like to keep it!”

In August, the Bolt Health program scheduled a follow-up blood test for me and sure enough, my Testosterone levels had been boosted from 415 to 730ng/dL, bringing me from the low side of normal to the higher side.

Many labs define “normal” as anywhere between 300 and 1000, which seems strange to me given the huge effect this hormone has on your wellbeing. It’s a bit like saying “Most cars have between 90 and 300 horsepower, so it doesn’t really matter what engine you have”

I mean yeah, either one will still get you down the road, but which one would you rather be driving?

Since then, it has just been more of the same good results. My improvements ramped up and then just stayed there – so I’m operating at a new, much higher and more enjoyable level of functioning. Energy and motivation are no longer a problem, and I even find myself willing to make longer-term plans again (before this everything beyond same-day planning felt overwhelming). And my body seems to just want to gain strength and size with any excuse. Heavy weights feel lighter and the hard manual labor I still like to spend my time on feels easier for longer. It’s nice to be young again!

When you dig into the details, hormone replacement is mired in a soup of both real and incorrect information about both its benefits and its risks. And then our well-meaning medical establishment locks this whole container of soup deep in the cabinet with a label that says, “Needs Further Study”. But if you summarize the findings on both sides of the issue, you’ll see this:

The modern American Lifestyle is a Testosterone and Health Crusher. It’s a miracle that anybody feels good ever with the crap that people do to their bodies. So if you’re not already doing all the simple, natural, outdoor things that naturally boost your health, energy, and hormone levels, you’ll want to start with these first. You can find a pretty complete list on my oft-cited Badassity Tracker page.

Since I was already doing all of these things pretty consistently, I felt ready to take the next step and at least consider hormone supplementation. But wait, there’s more!

Many of the problems above are more likely to appear when the body is flooded with too much testosterone. In the bad old days, TRT was administered by sticking a pellet beneath your skin or injecting a large amount into the butt which then gets used up over the next several weeks. One friend recounted a story of extreme moodiness when the pellet was first implanted, ramping down to tiredness by the time the hormone was all gone.

More modern providers like Bolt have fixed this problem by breaking the dose into much smaller servings which you administer each day. The idea is that your levels remain stable, and you need a lot less overall which reduces side effects.

For my part, I have not had any of the negative side effects because I was a pretty ideal candidate in the first place: 50 years old with depressed Testosterone levels but an otherwise healthy lifestyle and no risk factors.

My hope in sharing this article is to be transparent and hopefully take some of the stigma out of this subject of other people who might benefit. Because in our modern over-connected world, everybody has an opinion on your life, even when you didn’t ask them.

And it’s not just men – many women in this same age group benefit from Estrogen replacement (and there are even interesting stories about female testosterone supplementation in certain situations as this author shares). The point is that aging is normal, but in some cases there’s a pretty easy way to make it slower

The great news is that Testosterone itself is a cheap and widely available substance, typically under $50 per month even for people like me without conventional insurance or drug coverage. The expensive part (here in the US) is just the doctor stuff – consultations, blood tests, ongoing analysis and prescription renewals and so on.

The company that I used is positioned as a premium provider, bundling these services along with a bunch of other men’s health perks and deliveries for a few hundred dollars, which is expensive relative to most other parts of my budget, but still cheap if I consider the life and financial benefits of being 20-50% more energetic and productive.

If you want to be on this program, your final decision will hinge on your income, insurance coverage if applicable, whether your existing doctor can already help you, and how much service and advice you’re willing to pay for.

Note: I decided not to become a Bolt health affiliate because I wanted to write this article without conflict of interest. And I can honestly say, Bolt’s product and service seem great to me because I know and trust the people who run it. But  it’s also the only one I’ve tried. So I don’t know much about the competition and there may be other good options out there. At the very minimum, you can always try one service and switch to another if you don’t like the first one.

I’ve got lots more to say on money and early retirement, and lots of interesting projects in the works now too. So I’m thankful to have stumbled upon this booster for all aspects of life, so I can do more of everything else, for even more decades than I had expected.

I wish this same type of good fortune for you, however you create it.

Many GPs are understandably cautious and often won’t prescribe testosterone beyond low “reference range” levels. That said, there’s solid evidence that appropriately dosed and medically supervised hormone therapy can be beneficial for people with clinically low levels.

I’m a woman on HRT and have seen objective improvements, including bone density. In my family, my husband and three adult sons (ages 36–76) are on testosterone, prescribed and monitored by a physician, with regular labs.

The literature supports this approach when clinically indicated: testosterone therapy has been shown to improve bone mineral density and lean mass, and in some men, quality of life and metabolic markers—without clear evidence of harm when properly monitored.

Sources include NIH reviews, Endocrine Society clinical guidelines, and articles in JAMA and NEJM, all of which emphasize careful patient selection, dosing, and follow-up rather than blanket rejection or casual prescribing.

Interesting. I know very little about this topic, but as I read my thoughts immediately went to the evolutionary biologist Robert Sapolsky and his book The Trouble With Testosterone. I would encourage you to go down that pathway and add it into your thinking. I’m curious what the Bolt people would say to these arguments.

It has been some time since I read the book so I got some LLM summaries to refresh me on why many evolutionary biologist consider testosterone an expensive biological tax. I’m going to paste some of it here:

In the wild, maintaining high testosterone levels is akin to driving a car with the engine red-lining. It provides short-term power for mating and fighting, but it wears down the machinery (the body) much faster. Here is a breakdown of the specific evolutionary costs Sapolsky and other biologists highlight, focusing on the immune system and metabolic “taxes.” 1. The Immunocompetence Handicap This is the central theory explaining why high testosterone is costly. The “Handicap Principle” suggests that because testosterone suppresses the immune system, only males with superior genetics can afford to maintain high levels of it. The Trade-off: Energy is finite. The body must choose between investing in survival (immunity, cell repair) or reproduction (muscle mass, aggression, mating displays). Testosterone forces the body to prioritize reproduction at the expense of survival. The “Honest Signal”: High T features (like a peacock’s tail or a stag’s massive muscles) are “honest signals” to females because they are dangerous to possess. The male is essentially saying, “Look at how strong my genes are—I can handicap my own immune system with this much testosterone and still be standing.” Parasitic Load: In wild primate studies, males with the highest testosterone often have the highest burden of intestinal parasites. Their immune systems are less efficient at fighting off low-level infections because their energy is diverted elsewhere. 2. Metabolic & Physiological Costs Beyond just the immune system, high testosterone extracts a heavy toll on the body’s daily maintenance. Metabolic Burn: Testosterone is metabolically expensive. It forces the body to build and maintain lean muscle mass which burns calories at a much higher rate than fat. In a food-scarce environment (which is most of evolutionary history), having high T is a risk; you are more likely to starve during a famine. The “Good Cholesterol” Crash: Testosterone generally lowers HDL (good cholesterol). Sapolsky notes that this is one reason why males across many species die younger than females. The hormone that helps you win the fight today clogs your arteries for tomorrow. 3. Behavioral “Taxes” High testosterone lowers the threshold for risk-taking, which carries a direct survival cost. Injury and Mortality: High-T males are more conspicuous and more likely to engage in risky confrontations. In the wild, “winning” a fight often leaves a victor injured, making them susceptible to infection (which their T-suppressed immune system is now less equipped to fight). Parental Investment: Evolutionarily, there is often an inverse relationship between testosterone and parental care. High T drives mating effort (seeking new partners) rather than parenting effort (caring for offspring). In species where offspring need high investment, high T can actually be an evolutionary disadvantage if the offspring die from neglect. Summary of the Trap The “trouble” Sapolsky identifies is that while high testosterone might help a male pass on genes (by winning a mate), it actively works against his staying alive. The Irony: Pro-TRT (Testosterone Replacement Therapy) arguments often frame high T as the key to “health” and “vitality.” From an evolutionary standpoint, nature views high T as the exact opposite: a calculated health risk taken solely to reproduce before you die.

I hope this is good food for thought and discussion. Thanks for your years of great blogging MMM!

Did you do any research on dosing daily versus once or twice a week? My concierge physician has me on twice per week and I’m curious about how it might affect me if I switched that to a daily smaller dose. Any insights you have?

Testosterone cypionate (most common, what MMM is using) and enanthate (another commonly used ester) have a half-life of around 10 days, meaning that 10 days after your dose about half of it will be left. After a few weeks of weekly dosing the levels stabilize (you can math this out using mg if you want). There’s zero reason to dose daily. I actually tested twice-weekly dosing vs weekly with blood testing and there was no difference in my levels. Weekly is more than fine and you won’t notice any fluctuations. It’s pretty common for people to dose every other week, but weekly is more than sufficient to maintain consistent levels.

#8523. Direct Stock Purchase Plans Charge Fees – A $0-Commission Broker Usually Costs Less

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

A direct stock purchase plan lets you skip the broker, but it can charge you for each purchase, each dividend reinvested, and each sale. It also buys only at set times. Use a $0-commission brokerage account instead, unless the plan charges nothing to buy and its discount on reinvested dividends will outweigh the sale fee.

A transfer agent such as Computershare, the firm that keeps a company’s shareholder records, runs the plan. Its fees take the biggest bite out of small, regular purchases, like $50 a month into a child’s account or a favorite dividend payer.

Hershey’s plan shows how the fees add up. The first purchase, $250 at minimum, carries no fee. After that, each automatic monthly purchase costs $2.50 plus 5 cents a share, so each $50 purchase loses more than 5% to fees. Reinvesting a dividend costs 5% of it, up to $5, plus 5 cents a share. Selling costs at least $15 plus 12 cents a share, more than 7.5% of a $200 holding.

A brokerage account with $0 commissions and fractional shares, which let $50 buy part of a share, puts the whole $50 into Hershey stock and lets you sell online with no commission. Plans also usually buy and sell at set times, at an average market price, rather than at a price or moment you pick, the SEC notes.

Before you enroll, find the plan’s fee schedule on the company’s investor relations site and check the setup fee and what each purchase, reinvested dividend, and sale costs. A few plans give reinvested dividends a discount on the shares they buy. Omega Healthcare Investors, for one, currently sets a 1% discount on the new shares its plan issues for reinvested dividends. A plan like that beats a $0-commission broker when buying and reinvesting cost nothing and the discount adds up to more than the fee to sell.

For any other stock, open a brokerage account and buy the shares there, then turn on dividend reinvestment for them.

Open the account at one of the best online brokers for free stock trading.

#8522. JAL Business Class via Multiple Transfer Partners

World-class Japanese hospitality at a fraction of the cash price via partner bookings

Picture this: you're settled into your own private suite at 37,000 feet somewhere over the Pacific. The door closes. A flight attendant in a crisp JAL uniform offers you a warm towel and asks how you'd like your appetizer served. The flat bed is already made with a proper duvet. Outside the window, the sun is setting over the ocean. You're nine hours into a 12-hour flight to Tokyo, and you feel more rested than you did when you boarded. This is JAL's Sky Suite — one of the most celebrated business class products in the world — and with the right travel rewards strategy, your family can experience it for a fraction of what everyone else is paying. Here's the math that stops people cold: a round-trip business class ticket from San Francisco to Tokyo on JAL typically retails for **$5,000 to $10,000 per person**. That's not a typo. Premium transcontinental fares are genuinely that expensive, and most people simply accept that they'll never sit up front on a 12-hour flight across the Pacific. But the ChooseFI community knows better. That same seat — the same flat bed, the same Champagne, the same Sky Suite cocoon — is available for **60,000 miles** when booked through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. At a retail value of $5,000 to $10,000, you're looking at **8.3 to 16.7 cents per point** in value. For context, most travel rewards experts consider anything above 1.5 cents per point a good redemption. This one can be up to *eleven times* that benchmark. The pricing inefficiency exists because partner award programs — like Alaska and American — use fixed award charts that were negotiated years ago, before JAL's hard product became one of the most sought-after cabins in the sky. JAL hasn't raised these partner pricing levels proportionally as cash fares have climbed. The gap between what you pay in points and what the market charges in dollars is enormous, and it's yours to exploit right now. This isn't a loophole that's about to close tomorrow. It's a structural feature of the loyalty system — one that rewards people who understand how to use their points strategically rather than burning them on domestic economy upgrades. For anyone on the path to financial independence, where every dollar and every point is treated with intention, this is exactly the kind of asymmetric opportunity worth understanding.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: JAL's own frequent flyer program is not where you want to book this award. This is the aha moment that separates casual points users from strategic ones.

JAL operates its own loyalty program — JAL Mileage Bank — but it charges significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often running $100 to $500 or more per ticket. When you book JAL business class through JAL Mileage Bank itself, those surcharges erode a substantial portion of your points value before you even leave the ground. The ChooseFI community's editorial guidance here is unambiguous: book JAL through partner programs to avoid this tax on your redemption.

There are two primary programs where you can book JAL business class at 60,000 miles round-trip on the transpacific route:

Alaska Mileage Plan prices JAL business class at 60,000 miles for a round-trip between North America and Japan. Alaska is a oneworld partner of JAL and honors JAL's genuinely strong award availability. Critically, Alaska does not pass through JAL's fuel surcharges to awards booked through Mileage Plan. This is a massive advantage.

American AAdvantage also prices the same route at 60,000 miles round-trip. Both programs use fixed award charts, meaning the price doesn't fluctuate with demand the way cash fares do — a $10,000 ticket at peak cherry blossom season costs exactly the same points as a ticket in a slower travel month.

Neither Alaska Mileage Plan nor American AAdvantage is a direct transfer partner from the major US bank programs in the same way Chase or Amex partners work. However, you have real pathways:

For Alaska and American miles specifically, the strongest earning strategies involve:

Both Alaska and American use fixed award charts — meaning the price in miles is the same regardless of how high the cash price climbs. This is the structural inefficiency at work. A seat that retails for $10,000 during peak season still costs 60,000 miles. The chart doesn't care about demand; it just prices by region and cabin. As long as JAL releases availability — and they do — the gap between cash cost and points cost remains enormous.

JAL also allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award, which means you can potentially add a stop in Tokyo itself while continuing to another Japanese city, or fly into one city and out of another — all at no additional miles cost.

This is the cardinal rule of all travel rewards bookings: never transfer points until you have confirmed availability. Points transfers are generally irreversible.

Go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) to search for JAL award availability. Because BA is also a oneworld partner, their search tool shows you JAL award space. Search for your route (e.g., SFO to NRT) in business class. Any availability you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well. Look for "J" class availability, which represents business class award space.

You can also call Alaska Airlines at 1-800-252-7522 or American Airlines at 1-800-433-7300 and ask their agents to search JAL availability on your dates. Agents sometimes see space that doesn't show up online.

JAL's booking window opens 360 days in advance. For peak travel periods — Golden Week in Japan (late April to early May), cherry blossom season (late March to early April), and the summer holidays — availability disappears fast. Set a calendar reminder to search and book as soon as the window opens for your target dates.

For travel year-round outside those peaks, JAL is known for releasing strong business class availability, which is why this sweet spot earns a 4/5 on availability. You have real flexibility here.

Decide whether you'll book through Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage. Both charge 60,000 miles round-trip. The key differentiator: Alaska does not pass through fuel surcharges. If minimizing out-of-pocket costs is your priority, Alaska is the better choice.

For Alaska miles: Apply for the Bank of America Alaska Airlines Visa, earn the welcome bonus, and use shopping portals and partner promotions to top up. For American miles: The Citi AAdvantage Platinum Select or Barclays AAdvantage Aviator cards offer solid welcome bonuses. You'll need a minimum of 60,000 miles per person.

If you need to use the Capital One → JAL Mileage Bank transfer path, initiate the transfer from your Capital One portal. Transfers post in 1-2 days. Note that booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly will incur fuel surcharges.

For Alaska: Call 1-800-252-7522 or book online at alaskaair.com/partner-awards. Online booking of JAL awards through Alaska can be hit-or-miss; calling is often more reliable.

For American: Book at aa.com or call. American's website allows partner award searches, though calling often surfaces additional availability.

Once booked, confirm your ticket number, that the cabin shows as "Business" (not an upgrade), and request your preferred meal. JAL offers Western and Japanese meal options — request ahead. Your seat assignment on the 787-9 Sky Suite or 777-300ER Apex Suite can be made at booking.

The core arbitrage here is the difference between booking through JAL's own program versus booking through oneworld partner programs. JAL Mileage Bank imposes significant fuel surcharges on its own award tickets — often $100 to $500 per ticket — which erodes the points value substantially. But Alaska Mileage Plan and American AAdvantage can book the exact same JAL-operated flights with zero fuel surcharges because they use their own award charts and pricing rules. You are flying on JAL's aircraft with JAL's crew and JAL's business class product, but paying through a partner program's more favorable pricing. This is the same structural mismatch that creates sweet spots throughout the oneworld alliance — the booking program's pricing does not match the operating airline's product quality.

Let's run the numbers on a specific scenario that thousands of ChooseFI members have used as a benchmark: San Francisco (SFO) to Tokyo Narita (NRT) in JAL business class, round-trip for two people.

A quick search on Google Flights or JAL's own website for this route in business class will typically show cash prices ranging from $5,000 to $10,000 per person — let's use $7,000 as a reasonable midpoint for this example. For two people, you're looking at a $14,000 cash outlay before you even think about hotels in Tokyo.

Booked through Alaska Mileage Plan: 60,000 Alaska miles per person, round-trip. For two travelers, that's 120,000 Alaska miles total, plus taxes and fees (which Alaska keeps minimal for JAL awards, typically under $100 for the pair).

The CPP math: $7,000 in value ÷ 60,000 miles = 11.7 cents per point — squarely in the middle of the 8.3-to-16.7-cent range and nearly 8 times what most people get burning points on domestic economy tickets.

On the 777-300ER, you may get the Apex Suite — a staggered configuration with direct aisle access from every seat and a similarly flat, private sleeping environment.

Beyond the hardware: JAL's service is routinely ranked among the best in the world. The meal service for a 12-hour transpacific flight is multi-course, the sake selection is curated, and the attention to detail in Japanese hospitality culture elevates the experience above what the points price alone suggests.

You'll also access the JAL First Class Lounge or JAL Business Class Lounge at Narita on the return — another perk included with your business class boarding pass. By the time you land in San Francisco after a flat-bed sleep and a proper breakfast service, you've experienced what most travelers save for a once-in-a-lifetime trip. With travel rewards, it can be your default way to cross the Pacific.

British Airways' award search at ba.com is one of the best tools for seeing oneworld partner availability without committing any miles. Use it to scout JAL space across multiple dates before you transfer a single point. It shows business class availability clearly and quickly.

JAL's award calendar opens 360 days in advance. For anyone targeting cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or Golden Week (late April to early May), you should be searching and booking at the 360-day mark, not 60 days out. These are the hardest windows to find availability. Outside peak Japan travel seasons, this is much more forgiving.

JAL Mileage Bank allows one free stopover and one open jaw per round-trip award. If you're booking through JAL Mileage Bank directly (accepting the fuel surcharges), you can fly into Tokyo and out of Osaka, for example, without additional miles. This is a genuine value-add for anyone planning a broader Japan itinerary — no backtracking required.

This is a small thing that makes a big difference. Request the Japanese meal option when booking. It's more authentic, better-suited to the overall experience, and — in the ChooseFI spirit of intentionality — it's why you chose this airline over a generic carrier.

This is the single most common and most painful mistake. Points transfers are almost always one-way and irreversible. Never, under any circumstances, transfer points to a program before you have verbal or written confirmation of the award space you intend to book.

As emphasized in the program overview: JAL charges significant fuel surcharges on awards booked through its own program — $100 to $500 or more. For transpacific routes, always book through Alaska or American to avoid these fees. The data is explicit on this point.

If you do earn JAL Mileage Bank miles directly, note that they expire 36 months from the date earned on a rolling basis. If you let a balance sit idle, you may lose miles before you've accumulated enough to book. Keep the balance active through small purchases or partner activity.

This sweet spot is best suited for couples and individual travelers who are targeting Japan specifically — whether it's a bucket-list trip, a first visit to Tokyo, or a multi-city Japan itinerary. The fixed 60,000-mile price per person means that families with young children will need to accumulate significant balances (60,000 miles per ticketed passenger), which pushes the complexity and earning requirement higher.

You need a minimum of 60,000 Alaska miles or 60,000 American AAdvantage miles per person to execute this redemption. For a couple, that's 120,000 miles — achievable with two well-chosen credit card welcome bonuses plus some additional earning through everyday spending or partner promotions.

This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

This redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. New I bonds earn 5.51% a year for their first six months. That’s inflation plus a 1.40% fixed rate. Your bond keeps that 1.40%, the highest since 2006, for 30 years. If you won’t need the money for a year, buy up to $10,000 at TreasuryDirect this year and another $10,000 from January through April.

You can’t control inflation, but the month you buy decides your fixed rate.

The inflation rate follows consumer prices. A new one takes effect every May 1 and Nov. 1, and your bond switches to the newest every six months, counted from the month you bought it. The fixed rate is set for each six-month buying window, then stays with your bond until it stops earning interest at 30 years.

For bonds bought from November 2026 through April 2027, Treasury set the fixed rate at 1.40%, up from 0.90%. That’s the highest since November 2006. The current inflation rate adds about 4.1% a year, for a total of 5.51%.

Say you buy a $10,000 I bond this November. At 5.51%, it earns about $275 in its first six months. After that, each new rate adds your 1.40% to the latest inflation rate. If inflation runs 3% a year, that comes to about 4.4%, and if inflation drops to zero, the bond still earns 1.40%. Either way, your bond earns about $50 a year more than a $10,000 bond bought in October, whose fixed rate is 0.90%.

You buy I bonds in an account at TreasuryDirect, the Treasury’s website, up to $10,000 per person each calendar year. A purchase this November or December counts toward 2026’s limit, so you can buy another $10,000 under 2027’s limit from January through April, at the same 1.40%. Interest counts from the first day of the month your purchase posts to your account, so buying late in the month costs you nothing.

Put in only money you can leave alone for at least a year. You can’t cash an I bond for 12 months, and cashing one before it’s five years old costs the last three months of interest.

Buy the first $10,000 by Dec. 31, then the second by April 30, before a new fixed rate takes effect on May 1.
