Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed quickly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

Use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move quickly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

Don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Don't earn Marriott Bonvoy points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

The ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

Minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

For the ChooseFI traveler who's been building transferable points for a year or two and wants to see what this system is truly capable of, this redemption is the answer.

This redemption is rated **Hard** — and that rating is honest. It earns that designation from three compounding challenges, not just one. **Challenge 1: Finding availability on multiple segments simultaneously.** Business class award space on popular long-haul routes is limited. Finding saver-level availability on one segment is manageable. Finding it on two connected segments, with dates that create a coherent stopover itinerary, requires persistence and flexibility. This is the primary barrier. **Challenge 2: Understanding Aeroplan's routing logic.** Aeroplan's stopover rules, multi-city booking interface, and the distinction between how partner awards are priced require more than surface-level familiarity with the program. A misunderstanding of how the stopover is added can result in a significantly higher points cost or a booking that doesn't reflect your intended itinerary. **Challenge 3: Coordinating the transfer timing.** With a 355-day booking window and fast-moving business class availability, the timing of your point transfers requires active management — particularly if you're not using Chase's instant transfer speed. ## Three Tips to Overcome These Challenges 1. **Start your availability research 60–90 days before the 355-day window opens.** Know your target route, your preferred stopover city, and your date range before you ever log into aeroplan.com. Preparation turns a chaotic search into a focused one. 2. **Use united.com as your availability research tool.** It searches the Star Alliance network and shows you realistic inventory without requiring you to commit points. 3. **Don't be discouraged by the learning curve.** Every hard redemption in the ChooseFI community gets easier the second time. Plenty of members who now book these routinely considered them impossible the first time they looked. The complexity is real — but so is the $10,000 of value sitting on the other side of it.

Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

Set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

No, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

Aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

The best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

The Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

#8498. Jordanian Man Trekking 23,000Km From South Africa to Siberia

Saddam Al Alaya is almost a year into his attempt to walk 23,000km from Cape Town, South Africa, to Magadan, in Russia’s Far East. The 35-year-old Jordanian left Cape Town on January 1, 2026, on a trek that he estimates will take three years. He covered the 5,500km to Rwanda in nine months, so he is on schedule.

This year, Al Alaya has already passed through South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Zambia, Tanzania, Burundi, and now Rwanda. He expects to transit 18 countries in all, including his home country of Jordan, which he will cross from south to north.

Al Alaya grew up in Wadi Musa, beside Petra, and began guiding tourists around the famous archaeological site and the nearby canyons when he was about 16. He continued to guide while working for a business degree. He conceived the idea for this long walk in 2021, and spent almost five years organizing it.

Al Alaya meets a supporter. Photo: Facebook

Like so many adventurers, he wants to give his project a social angle, but Al Alaya seems particularly good at this. He founded an organization called Hike With Me, and many of his social media images show him glad-handing officials, walking with local people, or visiting regional schools. He often carries a white flag, symbolizing peace.

Al Alaya has official sponsorship from several Jordanian ministries, national organizations, and Jordanian embassies in various countries along the way. These have helped him with visas, security, and logistical support, according to the Jordanian News Agency.

Meeting some local people. Photo: Saddam Al Alaya

#8497. Draw Names Instead of Buying for Every Adult – Propose It Before Thanksgiving

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

In a big family, buying a gift for every adult adds up fast. Propose a name draw before Thanksgiving instead, where each person draws one name and buys that person a gift under a price cap you all agree on. Everyone gives and gets one gift instead of a stack, and that one can be better.

In a family of 10 adults, buying a $50 gift for each of the other nine costs every person $450, and the family $4,500 in all.

With a name draw and a $75 cap, each person spends $75 instead of $450, or $375 less, and receives one $75 gift rather than nine $50 ones.

In Deloitte’s 2026 holiday retail survey, 47% of respondents said they would rather spend more on one meaningful gift than give several smaller ones. A name draw lets everyone in the family give that kind of gift.

Propose the switch before Thanksgiving, and before anyone has bought a gift, so the family can draw names at dinner that day or online that weekend. Pitch it as less time in stores and more fun at the exchange, not as a way to save money. Then choose the format that suits your family:

A free site such as Elfster or drawnames will run a Secret Santa draw for you. Both can keep spouses from drawing each other and let each person make a wish list, so the one gift is something its recipient asked for.

Settle the rules before anyone draws. Set one cap for every gift and treat it as a limit, not a target. Decide whether the kids join the draw or still get gifts from everyone. Agree, too, that no one buys extra gifts outside the draw, since each one raises the bill again.

Send the whole family one message with the cap, the format, and a draw date already set, so all anyone has to do is say yes.

#8496. Bargiel Abandons Dhaulagiri Ski Attempt

Andrzej Bargiel and his team have also retreated from Dhaulagiri, citing bad weather and poor conditions. No one will summit Dhaulagiri this season.

Bargiel’s team, outfitted by Seven Summit Treks, reached Camp 2 while other climbing teams returned to Base Camp. The other teams turned back because of a lack of fixed ropes, and subsequently ended their expeditions.

But Bargiel still hoped to summit the peak and ski down to Base Camp. He planned to move up to Camp 3 yesterday and summit today, according to The Tourism Times. Bargiel did not share his exact location during the expedition, and his team often reported his progress with some delay. However, the skier reportedly retreated to Base Camp yesterday evening.

“Unfortunately, I had to give up on reaching the summit given the conditions we encountered,” Bargiel’s team quoted him saying. “Over the past few days, we’ve had significant snowfall accompanied by extremely strong, almost hurricane-force winds, and this created a high avalanche risk, which was the main reason I decided to turn back.”

This aligns with conditions described by the rope-fixing team last weekend, when they stopped work on the route. Soon after, commercial teams pushing for the summit were told to return to Base Camp.

“On a positive note, I had a great ski descent from Camp 2, with plenty of fresh snow. We’re all safe and heading home, and that’s what matters most,” Bargiel said.

The skier will not launch any further attempts this season to ski Dhaulagiri. Seven Summit Treks has officially closed the expedition with a rare statement explaining their decision to halt rope-fixing work. They cited their “guide’s decision” to turn around after assessing that conditions were not safe on the upper sections of the mountain.

The expedition’s director, Chhang Dawa Sherpa, was countering accusations by climbers that the rope-fixing team had lost their motivation after Seven Summit Treks’ biggest clients abandoned their summit attempts. You can read the full statement below:

This year, the highest point climbers reached on Dhaulagiri was around 7,100m, only slightly above Camp 3. No one has seen the conditions on the traverse below the summit ridge and the couloirs leading to the summit area.

Dhaulagiri is the second 8,000’er that no client summited this season, after a record number of teams halted their Manaslu attempts because of excess snow on the route. Only the rope fixers summited Manaslu. Two Russian climbers eyeing Makalu also decided to go home. With no permits issued yet for Kangchenjunga or Lhotse, the only summit chance on Nepal’s highest peaks now lies with the Russian team on Everest.

#8495. Cyclist Beats Pony Express Horseback Record

Lachlan Morton has completed a 3,217km bicycle journey along the historic Pony Express route from St. Joseph, Missouri, to Sacramento, California.

His time, 6 days, 21 hours, 15 minutes, beat the fastest recorded horseback mail relay from 1861 by 19 hours and 45 minutes.

Pony Express Trail. Photos: Top, Lachlan Morton/Instagram. Bottom: Shutterstock

Morton crossed eight states, negotiating remote desert tracks, the Great Basin and the Sierra Nevada. He encountered freezing conditions, fierce headwinds, and sections of barely discernible trail where he had to push his bicycle.

Unlike the original Pony Express, which changed riders and horses, Morton cycled the entire distance himself. However, he used different bicycles and had a support vehicle carrying supplies.

Morton is an Australian professional cyclist whose career spans elite road racing, gravel competition, and ultra-endurance adventure cycling. Rather than focusing solely on traditional racing, he has become widely recognized for long-distance challenges.

On a small balance, that yearly percentage can be close to or above the 10% a year large U.S. stocks have averaged since 1928. Until it falls under 1%, invest through a broker with no account fee.

Acorns charges $4, $8, or $12 a month, depending on the plan, and Stash’s plan costs $12 a month, or $108 for a year paid up front. Those prices stay the same whatever your balance, so they take the biggest percentage of a small one.

At $4 a month, you pay $48 a year, which is 9.6% of a $500 balance. That 9.6% is nearly all of the 10% a year the S&P 500, an index of 500 large U.S. companies, has returned on average since 1928, according to data from NYU professor Aswath Damodaran.

Index stock mutual funds, which track an index like the S&P 500, charged an average fee of 0.05% a year in 2025, the Investment Company Institute found. On the same $500, that’s 25 cents a year against the app’s $48.

When you do the math, count every balance the fee covers, the app’s retirement account included, not just its regular investing account. A $12 monthly fee on $2,000 across both is $144 a year, or 7.2%.

Round-ups, which invest the spare change from each purchase, can be worth the fee while they’re the only way you’d invest at all. You can build the same habit for free, though. Check what your round-ups added last month, then set up an automatic monthly investment of that amount at an online broker with no account fee. Pick one that sells fractional shares, so even $20 buys a slice of a fund that tracks the S&P 500.

The fee drops below 1% a year, a tenth of the S&P 500’s 10% average, once your balance reaches 1,200 times the monthly fee. That’s a balance of $4,800 on a $4 plan and $14,400 on a $12 plan.

To set up that automatic investment, compare the best online brokers, or, to keep your round-ups, the best micro-investing apps.

#8493. Wildfires Force Closure of Carstenz Pyramid for the Season

All around the world, natural disasters are hampering climbing expeditions. The latest case is a series of uncontrolled wildfires in Papua that have doomed the fall climbing season on Carstenz Pyramid.

The region is facing severe, widespread forest fires that have blanketed the island in a persistent thick haze. The air quality and visibility have reached levels that make transportation, logistics, and climbing operations impossible, according to local outfitter Tropic Adventure Papua. Apparently, the effects of the El Niño phenomenon, known this year as the Super Niño due to its extraordinary intensity, are to blame. It has brought a prolonged drought and extremely dry air, diminishing hope for the rain needed to extinguish the fires.

By the time the situation became unbearable, the first groups of foreign climbers had reached Timika in Papua, but no one made it to the top during this season, which is now officially canceled.

Outfitters have already shared the news with their clients and are now placing their hopes in 2027.

“Our thoughts are with the local communities affected, and we’re hoping the fires are brought under control soon,” Garrett Madison posted on social media. Instead, they have set the dates for next year, with two trips in March and October.

Tragically, the situation in Papua is only a fraction of a major environmental catastrophe. Wildfires are sweeping through the Indonesian archipelago and affecting Malaysia and Singapore:

The harm caused to the fragile Indonesian ecosystem is incalculable. In recent days, a viral video of a young orangutan rescued from a treetop where it tried to escape with burned hands and feet has drawn attention to the disaster. In fact, a significant number of primates were evacuated by rescue services in Borneo. Some of them were returned to the forests as the fire receded last weekend, according to the BBC.

The intensity of the fires in Papua and the air quality can be tracked live here.

At 4,884m, Carstenz Pyramid (Puncak Jaya in the local language) is the highest point of Oceania and considered one of the Seven Summits. Located in Central Papua, and with a tropical climate, Carstenz can be climbed at any time of year. However, summit options increase in the less rainy months, from February through November.

Outfitters apply for permits twice a year. Political unrest has often kept climbers away in the past, and major mining operations limit ground access. Climbers are typically airlifted to Base Camp instead of trekking through the jungle.

#8492. In Your 50s, Max Your Catch-Up Contributions and Build a Bond Cushion

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

From the year you turn 50, catch-up rules let you add $8,000 a year to a 401(k) and $1,100 to an IRA beyond the regular limits. Raise your contributions to use them. Shift gradually toward bonds until a few years of retirement withdrawals sit in bonds and cash, so a crash can’t force you to sell stocks low.

Your 50s are the last decade when extra savings still have years to grow, and the first when a crash could hit just before you need the money.

The IRS’s catch-up rules stack the 401(k) catch-up on top of the regular limit of $24,500 a year. In the years you turn 60 through 63, the catch-up rises to $11,250 if your plan offers the higher amount. The IRA catch-up adds to the regular $7,500 limit.

At a hypothetical 6% annual return, an extra $8,000 a year in a 401(k) for the 10 years from age 55 to 65 grows to about $105,000.

To get the full catch-up, set your contribution rate to cover the regular limit plus the catch-up over the year. If your wages from your employer topped $150,000 last year, the catch-up has to go in as Roth money, taxed now instead of when you withdraw it. In that case, a plan with no Roth option can’t accept your catch-up at all.

Build the bond cushion gradually. Each year, move a little more of your savings from stocks to bonds, or send new contributions to bonds, rather than switching all at once. By your retirement date, aim to hold a few years of withdrawals in bonds and cash, since losses early in retirement do the most damage.

Start planning now, too, for when to claim Social Security and how you’ll pay for health insurance if you retire before Medicare begins at 65.

Raise your 401(k) contribution rate on your plan’s website before your next payday, since catch-ups come only out of paychecks and must go in before the plan year ends.

Home » Credit » 6 Ways to Help Your Child Build Credit During College

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That said, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

Fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like new credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most important issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

One step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you plan to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

Some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

Many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

In fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an issue with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

College students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

Either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

#8490. Russians Give Up on the Khumbu Icefall; Will Try Everest West Ridge Instead

The first steps on a lonely Everest were daunting for four Russian climbers, who tried and failed to cross the Khumbu Icefall. They adapted quickly, heading up to the Lho La instead and setting up camp at that high pass at the base of the West Ridge.

Andrei Vasiliev, Natalya Belyankina, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Valery Sipilov set off from Lobuche on their first round up the mountain last week. Their original plan was to attempt the Khumbu Icefall, which has no ladders or ropes at this time of year. They set off at 5 am on October 9, looking for a way through the maze of seracs and crevasses.

“At first glance, it appears to be pure, unadulterated chaos,” Sergey Kondrashkin later wrote. “Yet on closer inspection, one can discern distinct sections. We opted for the central section, which seemed somewhat more solid — though ‘solid is a relative term…At least, it was easier to envision a viable path here between the seracs, snowfields, and ice walls.”

The recent snowy spell that hit Nepal filled many of the crevasses but also had a downside: loads of hard trail-breaking through deep snow.

Kondrashkin reported they crossed the most difficult terrain with only a few ropes in some sections and mostly moved as a roped team of four. “Time and again, I broke through the surface, sinking in up to my waist or even my chest,” he wrote. “By the end of the day, we reached an altitude of 5,700m, with still 500 vertical meters to go to the top of the Icefall and the biggest crevasses on the upper part.” They planted their tent on a small, flat platform.

“Conditions did not improve on the following morning,” Natalya Belyankina reported. “We ran out of steam on the second day, having gained only 100m in elevation after six hours, so we decided to head back down.”

The Russian team in the Khumbu Icefall on Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

However, they had food for four days, so instead of returning to Lobuche, they retraced their steps across the Icefall in three hours (they had spent one day and a half going up) and pitched the tent right below the high pass known as Lho La.

That was their second potential route. The Lho La is the col between Khumbutse, a lesser peak that rises to the left, and the characteristic pyramidal peak known as Everest’s West Shoulder. Lying on the border between Nepal and Tibet, it gives access to the very long West Ridge to the summit. It is also the route that Jost Kobusch will attempt in two months’ time. The German is on his fourth attempt to solo Everest in winter.

The Russian team’s tent in front of the wall leading to the Lho La between Nepal and Tibet. Photo: Natalya Belyankina/Instagram

Progress up the Lho La was fast, unlike the Icefall. The team completed the mixed terrain of the 600m wall in a single day, then pitched their tent on the col. On the fourth day, they scouted the terrain above and went to the base of the West Ridge, before returning to Lobuche for now, Alpymon reported.

The Russian team on a lonely Everest. Photo: Natalya Belyankina

The climbers loved the experience of being completely alone on Everest. “Groups of trekkers only make it as far as that famous rock — joking, laughing, and congratulating one another,” Belyankina recalled. “Just yesterday, near the Everest Base Camp rock, a young man was playing the saxophone. It sounded wonderful. But once we cross a couple of moraines, that’s it — we’re all alone on the mountain.”

Get the Capital One Venture X Business if your business will book at least $300 of travel a year through Capital One Business Travel. Its $300 credit and 10,000 anniversary miles return $400 toward travel each year, more than the $395 fee. Otherwise, take the $95 Venture Business, which earns the same 2 miles per dollar.

Premium travel cards charge a big fee up front and leave a business to earn it back through perks it may never use. The Capital One Venture X Business ties that payback to one habit, booking trips through Capital One Business Travel, since its $300 yearly credit works nowhere else. With the 10,000 miles it adds after each account anniversary, which Capital One values at $100 toward travel, the card returns $400 a year from its second year against its $395 fee.

Capital One, the McLean, Virginia, bank behind the Venture and Spark cards, opened the Venture X Business to all eligible business owners in September 2023. The Fortune 500 company says it serves more than 100 million customers, and it calls Capital One Business Travel the only free booking platform from a traditional card issuer designed for business owners.

The Venture X Business costs $300 a year more than the $95 Venture Business, which earns the same 2 miles per dollar on everyday purchases. The extra $300 buys higher travel earning, a yearly credit, anniversary miles, lounge access, and a bigger welcome offer.

Every purchase earns at least 2 miles per dollar, with no cap or categories to track, and employee cards earn for the business. Bookings through Capital One Business Travel earn more:

The higher rates cover only what you pay the booking site, so hotel incidentals and upgrades earn 2 miles per dollar. At a cent a mile toward travel, $2,000 of hotel stays booked there earn 20,000 miles, worth $200, while the same stays booked directly earn 4,000 miles, worth $40.

The booking site sells flights on more than 200 airlines, Southwest among them, and rooms at more than 1 million hotels. If a flight, hotel, or rental car you booked there turns up cheaper elsewhere within 24 hours of booking, Capital One refunds the difference on eligible bookings as a travel credit. Owners can also cap the prices and fare classes employees book and name admins to manage trips.

Each account year brings a $300 credit for Capital One Business Travel purchases, usable on one booking or several. It expires the day before the next account anniversary, earns no miles, and comes back if its booking is canceled before then. After each anniversary, starting with the first, the account also gets 10,000 bonus miles.

Together they return $400 a year against the $395 fee, but only the miles come without effort. Count the credit only if the business would book $300 of travel there anyway, the test any annual fee credit card has to pass. In the first year, before any anniversary miles, the credit offsets all but $95 of the fee, which the welcome offer can cover.

The perks, mostly for the primary cardholder:

The two free Priority Pass guests set it apart from the personal Venture X, whose cardholders pay $35 for each.

New cardholders can earn 150,000 miles after spending $40,000 on purchases in the first 4 months, plus another 150,000 miles and a $1,000 Capital One Business Travel credit at $120,000 in that window. The first tier alone takes about $10,000 of card spending a month. The $1,000 credit expires 16 months after the account opens, and current or former Capital One business cardholders may not qualify.

A mile is worth a cent when it pays for travel, the rate behind Capital One’s $100 figure for the anniversary miles. Get that rate by paying with miles on Capital One Business Travel, or by charging travel anywhere to the card and redeeming miles against it within 90 days, in full or in part.

Transfers can get more from a mile. Miles move to more than 15 airline and hotel programs, most airlines at one to one, so 1,000 miles become 1,000 Air Canada Aeroplan points. Emirates, EVA Air, and Japan Airlines give 1.5 miles for every 2, JetBlue 3 points for every 5, and Accor 1 point for every 2, while I Prefer Hotel Rewards gives 2 points per mile.

Covering a $400 fare at a cent a mile takes 40,000 miles, so transferring to an airline partner pays off when the airline prices the same seat at fewer miles, counting any taxes it charges in cash. Transfers can’t be undone, so confirm the seat first. Cash and gift cards pay rates Capital One sets and can change, and miles last as long as the account stays open.

The Venture X Business works like a charge card, with no preset spending limit and a balance due in full each month. What you can spend changes with your spending, payment history, and credit profile, and it isn’t unlimited. Pay Over Time lets you carry part of the balance, up to a limit Capital One sets, at a 25.99% variable APR (annual percentage rate).

There’s no foreign transaction fee. A late payment costs 2.99% of the unpaid part of the minimum payment, a cash advance costs $5 or 5%, whichever is greater, and balance transfers aren’t allowed.

Capital One asks for excellent credit, and the person who applies is liable for every charge along with the business, employee cards included. Late or missed payments may appear on that person’s personal credit report. Sole proprietors can apply with a Social Security number instead of an EIN, the federal tax ID number most businesses use.

For a business that will book its travel through Capital One, the Venture X Business has no net cost from its second year, since its $300 credit and 10,000 anniversary miles return more than the $395 fee. Every purchase also earns at least 2 miles per dollar, the owner gets Capital One’s lounges and Priority Pass with two free guests, and the booking site keeps employees within the owner’s limits.

It’s the wrong card for a business that books with a travel agent or directly with airlines and hotels, since its credit would go unused, or one that needs months to pay off big purchases. A business that won’t use Capital One’s booking site does better with the $95 Venture Business, which earns the same 2 miles per dollar on everyday purchases for $300 less a year. Before applying, add up last year’s flights, hotels, and rental cars. If $300 or more of them could have gone through Capital One Business Travel, the Venture X Business pays for itself.

#8488. Canada Coast to Coast Paddlers Begin Final Stretch

Canadian paddlers Will Vyse and Nolan Aziz — reduced to a twosome after Georges Kirijian left the expedition with an injury — are entering the final stretch of their mammoth 8,000km expedition from Tadoussac, Quebec, to Vancouver, British Columbia, on the Pacific Ocean.

After 184 days, including 34 days in Alberta, they crossed into British Columbia on October 10. This marks the final province of their trip. They have recently been paddling up the Peace River, which they describe as “long and arduous.”  The canoeists have covered well over 6,000km, and both they and their gear look suitably disheveled:

Once they finish with the Peace River, they have a meaty 17km portage to Williston Lake, the largest lake in British Columbia, before taking the southern branch of the Crooked River. After crossing the Continental Divide and completing the Giscome Portage between Summit Lake and the Fraser River, they will take the Fraser through Prince George and down to Vancouver.

Vyse and Aziz originally planned to end their trip in the town of Prince Rupert, but have since altered their route to finish at Vancouver’s Wreck Beach.

“Our reroute maintains a total expedition distance of over 8,000km, and upon completion will still be the longest ever recorded single-season canoe trip,” Vyse and Aziz wrote on social media.

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

#8486. Giant Crabs Complicate New Amelia Earhart Search

Researchers hunting for the wreckage of Amelia Earhart’s plane have followed new clues to a remote Pacific atoll, inhabited by giant coconut crabs so large and active at night that the team sleeps aboard its ship for safety.

In 1932, the American aviation pioneer became the first woman to fly solo across the Atlantic. Five years later, she and navigator Fred Noonan disappeared while attempting to circumnavigate the globe. After leaving Papua New Guinea on July 2, they failed to reach Howland Island, their planned refueling stop. The official account is that navigation and communication problems caused their Lockheed Electra to run out of fuel and crash into the ocean. The disappearance has produced decades of speculation about what happened.

Amelia Earhart beside her Lockheed Model 10-E Electra. 1937. Photo: National Portrait Gallery

One long-standing hypothesis, advanced mainly by the International Group for Historic Aircraft Recovery, is that the pair reached Nikumaroro (then known as Gardner Island), about 350 nautical miles southeast of Howland, landed on the reef, and later died as castaways.

A 17-person team from the Archaeological Legacy Institute and Purdue University arrived at the uninhabited atoll — part of Kiribati — this week after a 1,500km voyage on their vessel, according to the BBC and Purdue University updates. They are investigating the Taraia Object, an elongated shape in a lagoon first identified in satellite imagery in 2020 and visible in aerial photos dating to 1938.

Some researchers view it as a possible remnant of Earhart’s plane. Others consider it more likely a fallen tree or other debris. This marks the first authorized visit to the island in seven years, and the first to the Taraia Peninsula in more than 15 years.

The uninhabited Nikumaroro Island in the Pacific Ocean. Photo: Wikipedia

The work, which should take about five days, includes clearing vegetation, scanning for metal, and using dredging equipment to examine the object, which lies only about three meters from shore in as little as 1.5m of water, depending on the tides. Conditions have already limited boat access on some days, though organizers expect an update on the object’s identity within about 48 hours, according to Purdue.

The coconut crab has the strongest pinch of any crustacean. Photo: Reinhard Dirscherl via treehugger.com

The island’s coconut crabs, also called robber crabs, are the world’s largest land-dwelling invertebrates, with a leg span of up to one meter and a body weight of more than four kilos. They can lift objects weighing about 28kg, crack open coconuts, climb trees, and emerge at night to capture live prey such as rats and seabirds, as well as carrion. Expedition communications stated that the crabs’ size and overnight activity make staying on the island impractical, so the crew returns to the ship each night.

The same animals appear in theories about what might have happened if Earhart died on Nikumaroro. In 1940, British colonists recovered 13 bones near the remains of a fire. The bones were later lost, though some re-analyses of the recorded measurements have suggested consistency with a woman of Earhart’s stature.

The Taraia Object on a satellite image. Photo: Rick Pettigrew/Archaeological Legacy Institute

In 2018, the International Group of Historical Aircraft Recovery placed pig carcasses on a similar island and found that coconut crabs (along with smaller hermit crabs) stripped most of the flesh and dragged bones to burrows in less than two weeks. The crabs are not known to hunt humans aggressively. The primary risk is a powerful defensive pinch from their claws if they are handled or startled.

The survey of the Taraia Object began on Wednesday. The crew established a base camp, cleared overgrown paths, and prepared for their fieldwork.

Previous searches, including one by well-known explorer Robert Ballard, who first located the Titanic, have not produced any aircraft wreckage, and many experts continue to regard an ocean crash near Howland as the most likely outcome. The current team reports encountering some crabs during initial setup but described them as posing no threat to operations at that stage.

The Taraia Object’s survey has begun. Photo: Purdue.edu

Prior to that, Kris worked as a real estate agent, interpreter, and translator in criminal law. Now based in Madrid, Spain, she was born and raised in Hungary.

#8484. Image of Elephant Carrying Dead Calf Wins Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026

Federico Veronesi was following a family of elephants in the Huab River Valley of Namibia when he came upon a strange and tragic sight. A female elephant was carrying the stiff body of a deceased calf. The Italian wildlife photographer’s shocking image has become the Grand Title Winner of the 2026 Wildlife Photographer of the Year award.

Earlier, we reviewed the runner-up entries for this year, released back in September. One of those entries included Vegard Byrkjeland Aasen’s photo of an orca carrying a deceased calf, which it repeatedly lifted up out of the water. These striking images of animals mourning speak to the contest’s mission. Dr. Doug Gurr, Director of the Natural History Museum, says it strives to “demonstrate the extraordinary power of wildlife photography to help us see nature differently.”

Other category winners explore the relationship between the wild and urban worlds, document natural beauty, and capture more playful wildlife moments.

Winner of the Wetlands: The Bigger Picture category, Alex Visbal’s image shows how artificially dividing a Utah wetland has cut part of it off from freshwater, resulting in pink-producing, high-salinity microbes. Photo: Alex Visbal/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

While images like Visbal and Veronesi’s capture large scenes and massive animals, other winners focus on tiny, hidden natural worlds. Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas of Germany won the Rising Star Portfolio Award for his series exploring the smallest and least noticed animals.

As not all of our readers are as fond of arachnids as I am, we feature Tinker-Tsavalas’ whimsical image of a teensy springtail exploring moss, rather than his portraits of ground crab spiders or harvestmen. Photo: Alexis Tinker-Tsavalas/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Below even the insect level are the works of macro photographer Kutub Uddin. He won the Portfolio Award for his series of surreal slime mold landscapes. Like Tinker-Tsavalas, Uddin uses focus stacking to achieve incredible fine detail.

This fruiting slime mold looks like some sort of whimsical, slightly grotesque bonsai. Photo: Kutub Uddin/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Several winners focused on wildlife in non-wild settings. Loren Elliott won the Photojournalist Story Award for his series following the coyotes of San Francisco. There are around 100 coyotes living in and around San Francisco, and their relationship with human residents is close, but fraught.

There were several excellent shots in this series, but I would be failing you if I didn’t highlight this one. These two coyote pups live in a den on a golf course, leaving them plenty of golf balls to play with. Photo: Loren Elliott/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Across the world in Bangkok, common water monitors have also become city dwellers. Seth Forestson won in the Urban Wildlife category for his image of a lizard triumphantly bearing a fish through a public park. In the background, the city skyline rises in dramatic contrast.

Photo: Seth Forestson/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Meanwhile, the Plants and Fungi category winner comes from the weird world of mushrooms. On Mount Olympus, Agorastos Papatsanis used ultraviolet light to reveal the luminescence of Mycena renati. Commonly known as beautiful bonnet, the stems of these mushrooms glow a neon yellow.

Photo: Agorastos Papatsanis/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

The Young Grand Title Winner, who entered in the 11-14 year-old category, is Oscar Whitfield. In Zimbabwe’s Zambezi National Park, Whitfield captured the efforts of a dung beetle.

Ancient Egyptian cosmology drew parallels between the scarab beetle, pushing a ball of dung, and Khepri, the scarab-headed deity, pushing the sun across the sky. The dung beetle also plays a vital role environmentally. The way they process and bury dung reduces methane production and helps speed decomposition. Photo: Oscar Whitfield/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

You can view the full gallery on the Natural History Museum website. Tickets to the full exhibition in London, England are available here.

The full view of Federico Veronesi’s contest-winning image. Photo: Veronesi/Wildlife Photographer of the Year

Lou Bodenhemier holds an MA in History from the University of Limerick and a BA in Creative Writing from the University of Arizona. He’s interested in maritime and disaster history as well as criminal history, and his dissertation focused on the werewolf trials of early modern Europe. At the present moment he can most likely be found perusing records of shipboard crime and punishment during the Age of Sail, or failing that, writing historical fiction horror stories. He lives in Dublin and hates the sun.

#8483. The Saver’s Match Pays Up to $1,000 Even If You Owe No Tax

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Save in a 401(k) or IRA on a modest income, and you can get back up to half of your first $2,000. Claim the Saver’s Credit on your return through tax year 2026. From tax year 2027, claim the Saver’s Match instead, and the money goes into your retirement account whether or not you owe tax.

If you’ve assumed retirement tax breaks are for high earners, this one gives the biggest percentage to the smallest incomes. Yet only 48% of U.S. workers know the Saver’s Credit exists, according to a 2025 survey by the Transamerica Center for Retirement Studies.

The credit has a catch the match removes. It’s worth 50%, 20%, or 10% of up to $2,000, depending on income, but it can’t exceed your federal income tax. The match starts at the same 50% and shrinks as income rises, but it doesn’t depend on what you owe.

Say your income is under the cutoff for the top 50% rate in both versions, which is lower for the match than for the credit. Then $2,000 in an IRA earns the full $1,000 credit only if your federal income tax is at least that much. If you owe $600, the credit stops at $600, while the match puts the full $1,000 in your account.

You qualify if you’re 18 or older, not a full-time student, not claimed as someone’s dependent, and under an income cap that’s adjusted for inflation. Each year’s Form 8880 lists the credit’s limits, and IRS.gov’s Saver’s Match page lists the match’s.

Your own contributions to a workplace plan like a 401(k) or 403(b), or to a traditional or Roth IRA, count. Rollovers don’t, and withdrawals from the past few years shrink what does. An IRA deposit made by the April filing deadline can still count for the prior year.

Neither version is automatic. You claim the credit on Form 8880, and while your W-2 reports 401(k) contributions, tax software only learns about an IRA contribution if you enter it. The match works the same way, starting with 2027 returns filed in 2028, and your return is where you choose the plan or IRA that receives it.

Treat it as a match you have to ask for. Put the money in, then make sure your return claims it.

Savers without a workplace plan can choose from the best places to open an IRA.

#8482. Summits Begin on Ama Dablam, Late Fall's Most Popular Peak

With the failure of commercial climbs on Manaslu and Dhaulagiri this fall, all eyes now turn to the most popular commercial peak in the second half of autumn — 6,812m Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team already opened the route to the summit last Tuesday.

Unlike those two 8,000m peaks, where bad conditions prompted outfitters to abort the season prematurely, the seven rope fixers on Ama Dablam experienced light winds, sunshine, and good snow, which allowed them to fix 800m of rope in just five hours. Siddhi Bahadur Tamang, Lal Kumar Tamang, Dawa Paljor Sherpa, Lakpa Sangay Sherpa, Pasang Tenji Sherpa, and Namgel Dorje Tamang stood on top of Ama Dablam on October 13 shortly before noon:

Since then, workers have been hurrying to set up and stock three higher camps, while many climbers flock to Base Camp or acclimatize on nearby peaks before their summit push.

According to the October 13 update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism, 178 permits for foreign climbers have been issued for Ama Dablam. That will increase greatly over the coming weeks, since the high season continues until the end of November. In recent years, improved logistics and increased popularity have led to many more summits. Success rates are also far better than just a few years ago.

Last fall, according to the Himalayan Database (HDB), 273 foreigners attempted to climb — and all succeeded! They were supported by 399 Sherpas, including guides, high-altitude porters, and their helpers. The final summit numbers included the 273 foreigners plus 227 locals, totaling 500 summits, with a 100% summit rate. Two clients died: a Brazilian climber hit by falling ice on his way down, and a South Korean man who suffered cardiac arrest.

By comparison, in 2015, 76 foreigners and 47 locals summited — nearly five times fewer — and the summit rate was 71%. Certain things have not changed: Back then, the normal route was also fixed, and teams had Sherpa support. It’s the scale and the tactics that are different.

Ama Dablam Base Camp. Photo: Dominic Asselin

If Everest is to Himalayan climbing history what Mont Blanc was to the Alps, Ama Dablam is the Nepalese equivalent of the Matterhorn: a favorite of both climbers and outfitters, for different reasons.

Climbers appreciate its beauty — it’s usually considered one of the most aesthetic peaks in the world, despite its commercialization, with ropes, abundant Sherpa support, and helicopter transfers. Moreover, the views of Everest, Lhotse, and the surrounding peaks from its flat, snowy summit are breathtaking:

Its relatively low altitude means shorter acclimatization. Climbers usually do a trekking peak and/or hypoxic training at home as preparation. An Ama Dablam climb rarely requires supplemental oxygen — although it is available if needed.

Its convenient location in the Khumbu Valley on the way to Everest is a great asset, thanks to its many year-round accommodations, good infrastructure, an easy peak to acclimatize for, and a straightforward approach trek.

A crowded camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Lakpa Sherpa/8K Expeditions

For outfitters, Ama Dablam is a natural moneymaker. Its wide Base Camp on a dry, flat plain allows a large number of tents, a helipad, and the constant flow of supplies from the Khumbu’s main trail nearby. Yet the key to accommodating many climbers lies in fast expeditions. Once acclimatized, climbers can summit Ama Dablam and return down in three or four days — even less for the frequent speed climbers. That allows companies to reuse the tents and equipment many times through the season. Camp staff and guides are constantly working, with little downtime.

As for the climb itself, double ropes allow climbers to ascend and descend at the same time, maintaining a steady flow of people every day while the weather holds. Last year, there were 10 to 30 summits a day between October 12 and October 27, and nearly every day in November.

File image of climbers on Ama Dablam, progressing on fixed ropes. Photo: Explore-Share

Even during winter, which in Nepal officially starts on December 1, it is common for some teams to attempt Ama Dablam, especially before the end of the year. Expert winter climbers such as Simone Moro often mention the cold but stable and sunny days in Nepal in December. In recent winter attempts on Manaslu, Moro has acclimatized on Ama Dablam.

Nima Rinji, Simone Moro, and Oswald Pereira acclimatized on Ama Dablam in December 2024 before attempting Manaslu in winter. Photo: Manish Maharjan

Last year, the HDB only registered a three-member expedition that summited the mountain in winter. However, during the 2024-25 cold season, 12 foreign climbers and six Sherpas summited that December.

Ama Dablam was first climbed in March 1961 by Mike Gill and Wally Romanes of New Zealand, Mike Ward of the UK, and Barry Bishop of the U.S. via the Southwest Ridge.

Some local operators keep a functioning Base Camp and maintained route on Ama Dablam throughout December. Photo: Seven Summit Treks

With all this latter-day success and improved logistics, the biggest risk may be underestimating Ama Dablam. A high number of rescues have occurred in the last few years. Helicopters can perform long-line airlifts from Camp 3, but such options are not available in bad weather. The prospect of a rescue helicopter on standby in case of trouble, especially on the way down, may produce a false sense of security for those who find themselves at their limits but still decide to continue to the summit.

While the death rates on Ama Dablam are relatively low, it is not a peak to be trifled with, as the many cases of frostbite, AMS, and injuries from falling rock and ice attest.

A helicopter performs a rescue at Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Nga Tenji Sherpa

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

My goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:

When it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

On the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

The most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

The program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

The cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive plan for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

While Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable plan to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

One of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

The teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

MoneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

MoneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:

I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

The “Never 100” rule and “Straight A” strategy have become cornerstones of my financial habits, helping me live below my means and automate my savings and giving. It was perfect for someone like myself who didn’t want a complicated, jargon-filled financial class – and wasn’t going to sign up for an intense ‘shame & blame’ session either.

Personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

For those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured plan to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive plan to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

Regardless of which program you choose, the most important thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

He lives in Greensburg, PA with his wife and two children.
