#8434. Couple Cycle America's New Golden Gravel Trail

Colorado couple Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle have cycled 6,124km along the newly opened Golden Gravel Trail. The Adventure Cycling Association created the route this year to celebrate its 50th anniversary.

The trail crosses eight states — Missouri, Kansas, Oklahoma, Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, Idaho, and Oregon — and stretches from Cape Girardeau on the banks of the Mississippi River to the small town of Port Orford on the edge of the Pacific Ocean.

Most of the route, roughly 70%, is unpaved. It is the organization’s longest off-road cycling trail, 1,120km longer than the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route.

The Golden Gravel Trail route. Photo: The Adventure Cycling Association

Stennes and Doyle finished in Cape Girardeau after 73 days, averaging an impressive 80km and around 12 hours of pedaling per day. “About 90% of it is mental,” they told Heartland News. “You might be tired, but you just keep on moving.”

The couple are both experienced long-distance cyclists who have previously finished Montana’s Big Sky Spectaculaire in six days and nine hours in 2022 (a self-supported 1,400km ultra-endurance race), among other bikepacking trips.

Jules Stennes and Patch Doyle during the 2022 Big Sky Spectaculaire. Photo: Bikepacking.com

Likewise, the Adventure Cycling Association suggests riders should be self-supported for the Golden Gravel Trail. Riders are advised to carry two or three days’ worth of food for the route’s most isolated sections, and up to a day’s worth of water. This is particularly important in the more arid sections, such as eastern Oregon. In Colorado, Utah, and Idaho, the trail traverses subranges of the Rockies and crosses the route’s highest point, Cumberland Pass at 3,668 m, in Colorado.

Stennes and Doyle say their journey included thunderstorms, aggressive farm dogs, and “countless hills.”

Martin Walsh is a writer and editor for ExplorersWeb.

#8433. Climber Falls to Death on Ama Dablam

Search teams have found the body of Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, of Germany, who went missing after he reached Camp 3 on his way down from the summit. Evidence shows he fell 1,700m to his death.

Waschiczek was one among over 200 climbers who lined up toward the summit of Ama Dablam this past weekend. He reached the top on October 25 with guide Sonam Sherpa, but for some reason the two of them stopped descending at a rather high point on the mountain.

“The pair decided to stay at Camp 3 overnight after borrowing a sleeping bag and other gear from other climbers,” his expedition outfitter, Real Himalaya Nepal, told The Tourism Times.

Climbers above Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Dorjee Gyalzen Sherpa

According to the outfitter, the climbers prepared to continue down this morning. Lama asked his client to stay in place while he returned the sleeping bag to the tent where he had borrowed it. When the Sherpa returned, Waschiczek was nowhere to be found, but his crampons were still there, which suggested a freak fall. A search helicopter was called, and the remains of the climber were found this afternoon at around 4,500m.

Waschiczek is the first fatality on Ama Dablam this season.

Together with Manaslu, Ama Dablam is the most popular fall mountain in Nepal. The latest update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism on October 17 showed that over 300 foreign climbers had applied for a climbing permit. That day, the rope-fixing team opened the route to the top, and a massive summit wave started a couple of days later.

Virtually all foreign climbers are guided by one or two Sherpas, so the summit rates and numbers are remarkable. Local media estimate that over 200 climbers, among locals and foreigners, have topped out so far this season. Further teams should join them over the rest of October and November. However, no matter how tamed with ropes and anchors Ama Dablam gets, a fall from its steep slopes is usually lethal.

The upper part of Ama Dablam at sunset. Photo: 8K Expeditions

#8431. Loud Wealth vs. Stealth Wealth: Why Materialism Fades Over Time

I’m a proponent of stealth wealth. It makes for a more peaceful life with lower expectations and less scrutiny. The last thing you want to do is show off and put you and your family in danger.

Stealth wealth is also the natural endgame of following FIRE principles for decades. If you keep living well below your means, which is required to retire early, your investments will eventually compound faster than you can spend. At some point, your passive investment income and returns will surpass your living expenses.

So by default, every long-term FIRE practitioner eventually becomes a stealth wealth practitioner. Whether they mean to or not.

In private, you can do whatever you want. But in public, staying low-key is better.

1) Dress simply. No designer brands or fancy outfits. Clean, comfortable clothes are all you need. Think jeans, t-shirt, warm jacket, sweater, sneakers, baseball hat.

2) Drive an old car.  Driving a new car is stressful and can attract unwanted attention. If you insist on a luxury brand, try to keep it for at least 10 years.

3) Stay quiet about your spending on social media. Don't post vacation photos or the nice things you buy. If a tree falls in Hawaii and nobody sees it on Instagram, did the vacation still happen? Yes, and it was more relaxing.

Do these three things and you’ll join the Stealth Wealth club, a group of operators who move in and out of the shadows unnoticed.

Once you’re in, you’ll realize there are far more members than you think. That realization is oddly bullish. A lot more people are doing better than the media or politicians would have you believe. They’re just not wearing it.

In 8th grade in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, I wanted two things: to be cool and to have girlfriends.

My parents drove a 1976 Datsun with missing hubcaps. Getting dropped off in that car was social agony. So I had to find status elsewhere.

At the time, there were two ways to increase your coolness as a teenager: be a good skateboarder or dress in designer clothes. I chose both.

I still remember forking over 160 ringgit, about $64 back then (roughly $150 today), for a used pair of Armani Exchange jeans. 30-inch waist, 30-inch cut length, bronze eagle triangle on the back pocket. That was an absurd amount of money for a 13-year-old to spend on pants. But all the cool rich kids had them, so I had to have them too.

Then came the equally expensive Doc Martens. Then a Guess shirt. Looking back, nearly all my work and allowance money went to clothes and shoes.

And you know what? I enjoyed it. It made me feel good, and I was part of the cool crowd with plenty of friends.

Today, I couldn’t give two shitake mushrooms about designer labels. I want comfortable, practical clothes with zipper pockets so I don’t lose my wallet, phone, and keys. I cut my own hair to save time and money, and I usually cover it with a frayed baseball cap anyway.

So what happened between Armani jeans and black running pants?

I stopped needing respect from strangers.

I’m writing this post because of a clip from author Min Jin Lee explaining why some people with little money spend lavishly on material things. As personal finance enthusiasts, we shake our heads at such lavish spending. Don’t they want to eventually be financially free? But we’re missing something important.

Her point: when you grow up in a poor community, respect matters enormously. It becomes a kind of currency. And when you don’t have much else, you tend to overvalue it. So you buy the nicer clothes, shoes, watches, and cars, hoping they command respect, even if it means carrying credit card debt.

This resonated with me. Respect, especially for elders, is a big part of my culture. When people disrespect me online or in real life, it can be infuriating. In my younger years, I’d go after them to defend my honor.

When you think about it this way, materialism isn’t irrational. It’s a logical strategy for buying respect when you don’t have other ways to earn it. With this understanding, I'm going to try and be extra respectful to everybody I interact with from now on.

At 13, I spent a fortune on Armani jeans to earn respect from my skater friends and the girls I liked. When I started working in finance, I dressed to earn respect from my peers and bosses.

Then I left finance in 2012. Overnight, the nice clothes went untouched. I no longer needed respect from anyone outside my home.

Funny enough, they're all still hanging in my closet 14 years later in pristine condition.

Today, the only people I want respect from are my wife and children. Having respect from my parents and sister would be nice too, but we don’t see each other day-to-day so it’s no big deal if not. As any parent and provider knows, taking care of a family is hard work.

As a result, on our family trip to Las Vegas, I confess that a part of me felt disrespected when my wife gave me a bothersome look when I asked her to take a few more profile photos of me at Redrocks.

In that moment, my brain immediately pulled up the receipts. I agreed to this $7,000 trip despite being in a liquidity crunch. I went to bed at 2 am and still woke up by 6 am to get everyone breakfast. What’s the big deal?

Yes, I realize feeling disrespected in that moment might sound ridiculous. But that’s the point. A man wants to feel respected by his wife and children he provides for.

Reaching financial independence doesn’t eliminate the desire for respect. It just shrinks the circle of people whose respect you care about. The flip side is that when you don’t get respect from the few people who matter most, it stings far more than any stranger’s opinion ever could.

It’s worth doing an honest self-assessment of your spending on material things.

Maybe you genuinely love watches, cars, clothes, shoes, jewelry, or handbags. That’s fine, as long as you can comfortably pay cash and never carry a revolving credit card balance.

But if you’re buying expensive things you don’t even use or love, you may still be chasing status to earn respect. Maybe the midlife sports car is compensating for something. Maybe the designer wardrobe is a response to someone who once made an unkind comment about your body. Or maybe the nonstop social media highlight reel is an attempt to prove the middle school bullies wrong.

Whatever the reason, it’s worth exploring. Because the people you’re trying to impress are probably too busy trying to impress someone else.

For many of us in the FIRE community, the desire for stuff fades over time because the need for outside respect fades too. Once you’re living the life you want and own the things you need, strangers have nothing left to grant you. Nobody can hand you a better life than the one you’ve already built.

That’s the real luxury of stealth wealth. Not hiding your money, but no longer needing an audience for it.

Readers, did you go through a loud wealth phase when you were younger? What was your version of the Armani jeans? Do you think materialism is really about respect, or is something else going on? And now that you’re older, whose respect do you still care about, and how do you feel when you don’t get it?

Stealth wealth means nobody else needs to know your net worth. But you should.

#8430. New Cyclone Approaches Nepal

For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This new setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

Authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their plans and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those currently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his plans.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

#8427. Mont Blanc Has Grown Almost Two Meters — But Not in the Way You Think

These days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps. But strangely, Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, has grown significantly since its latest measurement in 2023.

Mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute). The new official altitude is now 4,807.47 meters (15,772.5 feet) above sea level.

However, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides. Measurements are carried out every two years, and each time the registered altitude varies:

Graphic showing the results of the last few measurements on Mont Blanc, by LaChangingMeteo

Mont Blanc’s “summit is constantly shifting,” Jean des Garets, chief geometer in the Haute-Savoie department, told Le Monde.  “Each individual measurement is not significant in itself.”

So, what’s with the yearly differences? Obviously, it’s the variation in the thick but ever-changing snowcap that covers the summit.

The mountain’s rocky summit measures around 4,792m above sea level. The snow cover varies with the seasons. The difference from the previous measurement shows that 2023 was much drier at summit altitude.

The survey team on itsir way to the summit of Mont Blanc.. Photo: ING

A team from the Order of Chartered Surveyors (Ordre des géomètres-experts) acclimatized first by climbing Bishorn (4,153m). They then spent some days measuring several points around the mountain. Finally, they climbed Mont Blanc via the normal route on September 15-16.

Once on top, they pinpointed the highest point using a GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) pole, which measures altitude in real time.

The recent survey featured an interesting novelty. In addition to altitude, the survey also measured Mont Blanc’s gravity by installing a gravimeter on the summit for the first time ever. This measured the force with which the Earth attracts the device. In so doing, they wanted to determine whether the summit has sunk, regardless of ice cover.

The gravimeter on the summit of Mont Blanc, September 16. Photo: ING France

“When the height of Mont Blanc changes, we can’t know for sure whether the ground or the rock has moved or if the ice has melted,” explains Olivier Jamet.

Gravity provides the missing information: mass. If the ice has melted, there is less material under the instrument, but the rock has moved closer to it. Distinguishing these two effects requires a model of the ice cap and the massif, and above all, repeated measurements at the same location. And the effort is worthwhile, especially now that the effects of climate change on Alpine glaciers are becoming increasingly apparent.

The gravimeter on the top of Mont Blanc measured the gravity at 9.7944689 m/s².

“For comparison, this value is 9.81 m/s² in Marseille (located at sea level) and 9.8043046 m/s² in Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet (580m above sea level),” ING reports. “This difference in value, even if it seems small, allows for the detection of changes in mass, particularly in the mass of the ice. Repeated over time, these gravity measurements will thus contribute to improving the determination of the altitude of the highest peak in Western Europe.”

#8422. Walking and Canoeing from Kansas to the Gulf of Mexico

In April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from New Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

Robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

During the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

“The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden shows the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

Cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They launched the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

It’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re currently on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.

#8418. Animal Attack Roundup, Oct. 27

Most victims of animal attacks around the world are not tourists but the people who live amid potentially dangerous animals all the time. Here are some incidents from the last seven days.

A tiger killed two farmers in separate incidents about five kilometers apart within 24 hours in the eastern corner of India’s Maharashtra state.

Sixty-year-old farmer Nana Kambadi was killed by a tiger while working in his field on Saturday evening. The following evening, Premila Mahadole, 40, was attacked while harvesting rice. Her body was later found in the field. Officials suspect it was the same tiger, but this has not been confirmed.

The back-to-back killings have thrown residents across the district into a panic, according to the Times of India. At this time of year, many are out in their fields harvesting rice at the edges of forests.

The death toll from human-animal conflicts in just this part of Maharashtra state has now risen to 35 in 2026, according to officials.

A family herd of wild Indian elephants. Photo: Shutterstock

An elephant killed a man who was trying to drive a herd of 23 elephants away from his village in Jharkhand state in eastern India. According to forest officials, the elephant seized Nicholas Topno, 40, with its trunk, dragged him nearly 500m, and trampled him. The herd, which included five calves, had been damaging crops in the area. Officials had been monitoring the movements for several days and warned residents not to approach. Our team has been monitoring its movement round the clock for the last five days, but some villagers still ventured close to the elephants,” forest officer Shekhar Singh told the Times of India. #8416. U.S. Trio Make First Snowboard and Ski Descent of a Near-7,000'er in Langtang

American snowboarder Nick Russell and skiers Adam Fabrikant and Billy Haas have just returned from Langtang with a first snowboard and ski descent of the south face of the formidable Dorje Lhakpa (6,966m).

The team climbed the peak, often known as the Langtang Pyramid, in two days in alpine style. They summited on October 20 and rode/skied down via the same line on the south face, while American photographer Blake Gordon and Canadian cinematographer Leo Hoorn filmed from a high camp.

On the summit of Dorje Lhakpa, October 30, 2026. Photo: Nick Russell

“The south face of Dorje was always the goal, and I’d been planning/dreaming of it for over two years,” Nick Russell told ExplorersWeb while on his way to the airport.

The expedition reached base camp on October 6, shortly after an intense storm blanketed Nepal’s mountains with heavy snow. For them, however, the snow was a blessing rather than a curse.

“The cyclone gave our zone some much-needed snow down low, and on the face, it allowed a clean descent (no down climbing, no rappels),” Russell said.

Sickness slowed the beginning of the expedition. “Three out of five of us, myself included, caught COVID,” Russell said. Luckily, the climbers recovered just as the weather cleared and winds dropped, followed by a string of perfect days.

After the descent. Photo: Nick Russell/Instgram

“Adam, Billy, and I all carried our own gear, set the tracks, and climbed in alpine style on the face,” Nick Russell said. The team had hired three Sherpa climbers (Dawa Geljee Sherpa, Kami Sherpa, and Nuri Sherpa) who helped the camera crew get their gear to a high camp, plus a base camp crew, outfitted by Shangri-La Nepal Trek.

High camp at 6,000m on the south face of Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The line of ascent/descent followed the snow from below 4,500m to Camp 1 (4,900m) by crossing an icefall. According to the team, this was the only real crux of the ascent, due to overhead serac hazard. At least, the exposed section was short — less than an hour.

On the first day of the summit push, the team continued to their high camp at 6,000m, below the col and at the base of the snowy face. Russell recalls the details of the climb as follows:

The south face is quite steep and sustained above the bergshrund, with sustained 45-50˚ and pockets of 55º, we estimate. The face had seen so much sun [over] the past two weeks that the rising conditions were the biggest unknown of the entire project.

We didn’t know whether or not it would be too icy to ride/ski until we got on the face. The snow was mostly firm, pretty much on the brink of being edge-able. It was two tool and crampon climbing the entire way, with no proper rests to take the pack off.

It took about 7.5 hours to climb the face, and we topped out around 1:30 pm. It took roughly 1.5 hours to descend, with breaks for the cameras to reset.

A climber leaves almost no tracks in the hard snow on Dorje Lhakpa. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

The three summiters started down from the top at the same time, Russell on snowboard and his partners on skis. It was anything but easy.

“The snow was more firm than I would have liked, but just edgeable enough to hold an edge,” Russell recalls. “Between the altitude, exposure below, steepness, and how firm it was, it was by far the heaviest line I’ve ever ridden.” He added that if the snow had been a little harder, they would have had to rappel down.

The hard snow on the upper sections. Photo: Nick Russell/Instagram

“You always hope for stable, boot-top powder, but that’s rarely the case at high altitude,” Russell explained. “Instead, you make the most of the conditions presented and try to do it as safely as possible.”

He added: “The entire line was a no-fall zone; one lost edge, and it’d be over. Regardless of conditions, it was a dream for all of us to ride off the top of a peak in Nepal.”

After a partial descent, the team spent the night at high camp, hoping to ride some interesting slopes they had spotted earlier, but finally decided to bail the next morning. “We were satisfied,” Russell said. They continued on skis/snowboard all the way down to the moraines below Camp 1 around 4,500m.

Childhood friends Fabrikant and Haas often partner up on major ski expeditions, mainly in Alaska but also in the Himalaya. They climbed and skied both Gasherbrums 1 and 2 without oxygen after climbing them in the same style in 2024, together with Brendan O’Neill.

“They are the strongest partners I’ve ever been in the mountains with,” said Russell, who has also climbed and snowboarded twice in the Indian Himalaya and twice in Nepal.

“I tried Dhaulagiri in 2022 with Blake Gordon and Dan Corn, but the difficult conditions that year coupled with the loss of Hilaree Nelson [who fell to her death while trying to ski down Manaslu] didn’t allow us to make very much progress,” Russell said.

“I’ve always dreamed of riding lines in the Himalaya, and this felt like a major step forward in my personal journey,” he concluded.

While this is the first ski and snowboard descent of Dorje Lhakpa’s south face, the legendary Marco Siffredi snowboarded the west ridge of the mountain in 1999, with Bertrand Delapierre. Siffredi perished shortly afterward on the Hornbein Couloir on Mount Everest. “Dorje Lhakpa first entered my psyche from Marco and Bertrand’s descent,” the rider recalled.

The south face of Dorje Lhakpa was only climbed for the first time in 2021, by Spaniards Mikel Inoriza, Iker Madoz, and Mikel Zabalza.

“I came across a photo of the south face and the American Alpine Journal article from the Spanish team’s first ascent in 2021,” Russell said. “The massive south face is visible from the Kathmandu Valley on a clear day, and it is honestly crazy to me that no one had skied it before.”

“Today,” he went on, “people are so hyper-focused on the 8,000m peaks (for good reason, I get it), but there are still virgin lines waiting for a snowboard/ski descent in the 6,000-7,000m range. It just takes a shit ton of work to make it happen.”

#8415. The Most Beautiful State: On the CDT in Wyoming

We crossed the border and I already felt more relaxed. The trail became more manageable, and I began to enjoy hiking again. We began to get closer to the Basin.

The Great Divide Basin is a long stretch of nothing but sagebrush for over a hundred miles. No trees in sight and barely any water along the way. Before we started our trek through the desert, we only had a day or two before we reached Rawlins, which became a haven for a double zero. Rawlins was more affordable than Colorado, and had a Pizza Hut, which JC and I discussed often during long hiking days. From there we set out.

120 miles. There were almost no natural water sources, so we had to rely on water caches. We planned our campsites around them, and timed our hikes in the early morning, late evenings, with a siesta during the hottest time of the day. JC got creative with our tent a few times for our siestas. On one particularly hot day, he threw the tent over a ditch, and we got to rest in the shade. Another time, he set it up in a way where it provided shade, but the wind blew it down on top of me.

When we were in Rawlins, I picked up my prized possession: a cheap umbrella from Walmart. I was so happy to get a little bit of shade as I was hiking, though the wind blew it around a bit.

The heat was so intense, just as it was in the desert in New Mexico. We passed sagebrush and mysterious holes, one of which JC found a black widow spider. We witnessed beautiful sunrises while listening to the worst fan fiction audiobooks we could find. The terrain, luckily, was incredibly flat, so the heat and exposure and the 28-mile stretch of no water at all were the only things we needed to worry about.

The first storm came as we had just left a solar well oasis, so we were able to turn around quickly and put up our tent near some trees. The second storm came as we decided to camp on a higher hill to enjoy the sunset. We had to quickly pack up and find a slightly lower spot and put up the tent as dark clouds descended. We huddled in the tent and waited for the storm to pass. And kept waiting. I unzipped the tent and stuck my head out. The storm that had looked so threatening had disappeared.

The last storm came on our last night in the Basin. Our last few days in the Basin were idyllic, as the temperatures decreased a bit and the clouds came in for a more overcast couple of days. It was perfect. As we were looking for a spot to camp, it seemed like there were three different storms brewing on the horizon. Luckily, the way forward didn’t have any storms ahead, so we sped up into the dark. We rushed as fast as we could, and JC found a spot with trees and a ditch to camp for the night. The storm raged on, and we were in the safest place we could possibly be.

Our trek through the Great Divide Basin ended in South Pass City, a tiny town that used to be a bustling hub during the Gold Rush. There was a store with some old-fashioned candy, where we chugged some root beer and tried candy cigarettes.

From there, we got a ride to Lander for the night. This was where we entered grizzly country, and we needed to get bear spray and an AdoTech at the outfitter. From there, we entered my favorite section of the whole trail: the Wind River Range.

So far, both New Mexico and Colorado, while very beautiful, were arid, rocky and kind of empty, with a lot of wide open spaces. The Wind River Range was lush, full of wildflowers, lakes, and trees, with sweeping mountainous landscapes. It was stunning and I could have stayed there so long. It really made me fall in love with hiking again.

JC promised to do the low routes with me, with the exception of the Cirque of the Towers. I wasn’t too sure about it, as people were talking about the descent from Texas Pass. I figured I would try the first pass on the alternate and see how it would go, as there was an alternate that would take me back to the low route. We started the alternate and began heading toward Temple Pass, which was not the best marked or maintained trail. JC and I spent a lot of time trying to find our way on the trail, and as we began to climb the switchbacks, the trail gave way to a high, eroded section that was barely trail at all. After a steep, gravelly section that seemed to go straight down, I decided to get off the alternate on my own. I was nervous to do this in grizzly country, but it would only be for half of the day. After that pass, we explored some lakes and stuck our feet in the frigid water.

The next morning, we split our different ways for the next ten miles. JC hiked on and did Jackass Pass and Texas Pass, whereas I had a calm, flat hike, through wooded alpine lakes with misty mountains against the against the overcast sky. Looking back, I am so glad that I took this alternate back to the CDT. It was one of my favorite days on trail. In the afternoon, JC and I met up again, and he talked about being underwhelmed by the Cirque of the Towers.

We hiked the rest of the Wind River section together as the trail winded through canyons and lakes. It felt like a dream, and as we exited the Wind River Range, we noticed a stark lack of lakes and wildflowers. Knowing that we were now in grizzly country made us more jumpy, especially as there were more cows making bear-like noises. We hiked through a wooded section and diverted ten miles off trail to get to the road to Pinedale.

I was so excited for Pinedale. JC and I were interested in seeing the Tetons, but we didn’t have time to do the Teton Crest Trail, so we decided to get off trail, rent a car, and spend a couple of days in Grand Teton National Park. We camped just outside of the park, and JC and I had a wonderful day, seeing the sights and doing much milder hiking. We drove around and ate snacks on Jackson Lake. It was nice to just enjoy each other’s company and be in way less life-and-death situations.

When we returned to Pinedale, we ran into NoCo, who had to get off trail due to an injury, and Leaky and Temu, who we hadn’t seen since Colorado. We also met a French hiker, Elvis, who worked hard to convince JC and I to never do the Tour du Mont Blanc in France. We spent the night at the bar, giving NoCo one last sendoff before he got off trail.

Before we knew it, we were almost done with Wyoming. The last stop before Idaho and Montana was Yellowstone National Park. I have traveled a lot, but I had never seen anything like Yellowstone. There were so many geyser basins and geothermal features. Yellowstone is one of the busiest national parks, but there were some backcountry spots where it was JC and I and the boiling, rainbow-colored pools.

As we hit Day 3 in the park, JC got the news of a family emergency back home. We got off trail for a day to figure out our options. Would JC need to fly back to the UK? It became a waiting game, and time began ticking on JC’s visa as well.

JC and I decided to keep going, knowing we may have to get off any moment due to the ongoing emergency. But we weren’t going to be able to do the whole thing. He came to an idea: we would leave Yellowstone, rent a car, and drive to Butte, MT and continue on from there. It was a dream of both of ours to see Glacier National Park, and we wanted to see it before it was impassable with snow. We took an amazing road trip through Idaho, stopping at Swig for a dirty soda.

And then we arrived in Montana, the last state of the CDT.

#8412. Saddle to Paddle: Bikerafting From Canada to Mexico

Pete Streufert and his friend Carter (no last name) are cycling 4,025km and packrafting 645km across the U.S. from Canada to Mexico. Starting in Glacier National Park, they will cross four rivers and six U.S. states to finish in El Paso, Texas.

Their route connects the rivers with long-distance cycling trails. This allows the pair to cross landscapes that would usually require separate trips by bike and watercraft. Streufert, a geospatial wildfire scientist and cartographer, came up with the route by combining existing GPS tracks and geographical data from Bikepacking.com, American Whitewater, and OpenStreetMap. He overlaid cycling corridors and rivers to identify where the two could connect.

Before starting the journey on September 17, he said they could find no record of anyone using this particular combination of rivers and cycling routes. So it is possible that they are the first to do so.

They started what they neatly call the Saddle to Paddle Traverse on September 17, from Glacier National Park, Montana, on the Canadian border. They kicked off the first packrafting section with a 115km descent of the North Fork of the Flathead River, which forms part of the western boundary of Glacier National Park.

From there, they followed the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route through Montana toward Jackson Lake, Wyoming, for 1,107km. Here, they hit their second paddling phase on the Snake River.

Every time they reach a river, the pair inflates their rafts, load their bicycles aboard, and paddle downstream. Then at each takeout, they deflate the rafts, attach them to their bikes, and continue riding.

After 130km along the Snake River, their route joined the SLoToJa cycling corridor. They pedaled through Idaho, Wyoming, and Utah. Here, a short connector track took them onto the newly developed Golden Gravel Trail. A further 860km of cycling brought them to Utah’s Green River.

They then paddled 328km through Desolation and Gray Canyons, including a handful of Class III rapids, and their only Class IV rapid of the trip.

Pulling their rafts out in Canyonlands National Park, they took the White Rim Trail to Moab. They are now taking a few days in Moab to “get all the mud off our bikes and escape the rain for a day or two before we keep heading south,” says Streufert.

From here, they will once again pick up the Golden Gravel Trail through the La Sal Mountains and across Colorado, then continue on the Great Divide Mountain Bike Route to New Mexico.

Paddling the Green River. Photo: Pete Streufert

A final paddling section on New Mexico’s Rio Chama will take them to the last leg of the trip, a 950km ride to El Paso.

The pair are riding Rodeo Labs Flaanimal 6.0 Steel, fitted with 29-inch Vittoria Mezcal tires, and using Kokopelli packrafts. The pair have described this as a “self-supported” route, although of course they’re replenishing their food along the way. They seem to combine camping with staying in towns.

View this post on Instagram See this post on Instagram

They should complete the journey within the next few weeks, within their two-month timeline. You can follow their progress here.

#8405. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8401. PCT Week 20: Home Stretch

📍 Mile 2,594.3 | 🥾 5.88 km | ⛰️ +339m / -55m

Rain had gently drizzled all night, and was still going when I woke up. I was eager to make it to town ASAP, in case it worsened, so packed quickly and was on the way as soon as I could. It was only five miles to Rainy Pass – apparently, a very apt name – and they disappeared quickly.

Unfortunately, getting a hitch didn’t come nearly as quickly. Cars zoomed past us, and we had to laugh at the number of times the drivers pointedly looked at the mountains on the opposite side of the road, as if they didn’t see us. I began waving to every car that passed and finally we had some luck: a van passed us, but turned around and came back to give us a lift. The driver turned out to have once attempted to hike the PCT, but had broken his foot on day three. Rough go. He was heading to Winthrop, which was further away than Mazama but had a bigger supermarket, so that suited us perfectly. And, by pure happenstance, Catch, Sabretooth and Shakedown happened to be trying to hitch there right as we were driving past; the driver stopped and let them pile into the back with me.

This resupply was a little different than usual. It was our final one of the PCT! After eating instant potatoes and tuna for literally every trail dinner since Julian in the desert, I’d finally reached saturation point and had to switch to ramen. We all bought a few of our favourite snacks and treats, and then had a fun little debate over near the alcohol about what we’d need for the terminus. In the end, we all got some form of bubbly, and a few of us grabbed some extras as well. Then we went in search of a town meal.

After a delicious burger at Three Fingered Jack’s Saloon, we were just preparing to try our luck hitching to Mazama when the heavens suddenly opened and rain bucketed down. It was torrential. Immediately we decided to go and grab a coffee at the bakery and wait it out. Of course, as soon as we had our coffees in hand, the rain stopped. When we did make it around to hitching, we didn’t have to wait long and got a lift with one of the first cars that drove by.

The hostel was practically crawling with hikers who, like us, were waiting out the bad weather but planning to start their terminus push tomorrow. In some ways it was overwhelming. I didn’t want to spend energy making new friends when we almost certainly were never going to see them again – a lot of people were heading up to Harts Pass, whereas we were going back to Rainy. But on the other hand it was nice to see a few familiar faces pass through. Apparently Sass and I had just missed Pieces, who’d left that morning. But Alice was still there, and then some hikers we’d been leapfrogging since the desert swung by to say hi after bagging the terminus. More and more hikers trickled in throughout the afternoon as we lazed on the outdoor couches beneath the dry marquee, enjoying the gas-powered fire at our feet and cooing at a puppy belonging to one of the trail angels helping out at the hostel.

📍 Mile 2,619.5 | 🥾 42.15 km | ⛰️ +1,777m / -1,235m

We’d signed up for a shuttle to Rainy Pass, but there were so many hikers heading back to trail this morning that we missed out on the first run. So we decided to try our luck hitching, in case that would get us there faster than the second run. We left early, hoping to beat other hikers who had the same idea, but when we reached the road we discovered we weren’t that early after all. There was no point in so many of us trying to hitch at once, so Sabretooth and I volunteered to do a coffee run while we waited our turn.

Coffees in hand, we were just leaving the courtyard of the Mazama bakery, when I tripped on a crack in the concrete. Before I knew it I was sprawled on the ground, embarrassed by the sympathetic “ooh”s from onlookers who’d seen me tumble. It was quite a fall. I had an open wound the size of an Aussie 5 cent piece on my palm, and I’d scratched up my legs pretty badly, too. It was a little ironic that I’d managed to sustain my worst PCT injury in town rather than on trail. I had, at least, managed to save my coffee – the cup was a little bent, but the contents were fine. But I’d been carrying Catch’s coffee, too, and it hadn’t survived. As I cleaned myself up Sabretooth ordered him another, and then I very carefully picked my way across the concrete and back to the road. By the time we got there the boys had gotten a hitch, but luckily the first car that saw us stopped and delivered us all the way up to Rainy Pass.

It was significantly colder at the pass. Sass and Catch were running laps of the car park to stay warm while they waited for us. We got on trail quickly, climbing higher still and yet naively hoping the day would warm up. Instead, we walked into lightly falling snow. It was magical, coating the ground and the trees in a light dusting of white. Then we arrived at the larches, which are conifers with needles that turn an indescribably gorgeous gold. Unfortunately, Cutthroat Pass was pretty socked in when we arrived, but we were in good spirits when we hit the 2600 milestone – only 50 or so to go! And only a mile or so later, the clouds began to disappear, giving way to a clear azure sky. Snow lay across the mountaintops as if someone had draped a cotton sheet.

We ran into a group of five hikers, overtaking them. They soon caught up with us again and we offered to let them go ahead, but for some reason they decided to tailgate us instead. So we stopped for lunch to put some distance between us. And it turned out to be a good call; a few rays of sunlight warmed us as we gazed around the mountains, taking in the colours of early winter. And when we set off again we soon reentered forest, so we were glad we’d stopped when we had a view.

The walking was nice and easy for several hours, but the final few miles of the day were a climb. It wasn’t a difficult grade, and we were soon above the trees and enjoying the mountain views once again, but I grew tired and was relieved when we made it to the top. Sunset seemed to be kicking off earlier than usual and the colours were unreal. The fading light turned the mountains indigo, which seemed to make the larches glow.

We arrived at camp, pitched quickly, and agreed we’d all be eating dinner from the comfort of our quilts, inside our respective tents. But that didn’t stop us chatting for an hour as we ate.

📍 Mile 2,649 | 🥾 49.9 km | ⛰️ +1,761m / -1,888m

I slept terribly. It was positively freezing last night, and we all woke up to frost on our tents. And to make matters worse, my inflatable sleeping pad was barely lasting for two hours – so I’d had to blow it up constantly throughout the night. I was glad when morning came and I could get moving to stay warm.

I’d been tempted to night hike last night, just because the weather was definitely closing in and I wanted to make it to Canada and back out quickly. But when we’d seen the trail continued along a ridgeline all thoughts of night hiking had disappeared. And this morning I was very pleased with that choice. The trail wrapped around the mountaintops, beckoning me forward into the beautiful day. The larches, interspersed with autumnal ground cover and evergreen trees, popped vibrantly against the pale blue sky.

We made it to Harts Pass mid-morning, and with the sun properly shining now took the opportunity to dry out our tents before setting off on the final push to the border. We all walked together, chatting happily. And then we started to come across PCT hikers who’d tagged the terminus and were now almost done with the 30-mile stretch back to Harts. Vibes on all sides were high; we were excited to be nearing the end, while those heading back were clearly relieved to be almost done and on their way to civilisation.

I was glad we’d waited out the weather; the mountains were gorgeous once again. A light layer of snow remained in the shadows of the peaks, in the little spaces that never saw sun. We crested Woody Pass just before sunset and were treated to stunning golden hour views of far-off mountain ranges.

Not long afterwards we ran into a group of hikers we knew who had just tagged the terminus. Catching up with them was great fun, although it did put us behind schedule. The sun was sinking rapidly. We pushed on quickly, but progress soon stalled when we arrived at a ridgeline where the blazing orange sun was setting to our left, and a glowing moon was rising on our right. How could we not stop and take it in? It did mean that our last 30 minutes or so descending to Hopkins Lake were in the dark, but it had been worth it. We’d heard rumours that a lot of people were already camped there, and that tent sites were scarce. But we found enough pitches for the five of us pretty quickly, and went to bed feeling like kids the night before Christmas.

📍 Mile 2,636.2 | 🥾 44.58 km | ⛰️ +1,666m / -1,731m

Today was the big day: after four and a half months, and hiking well over the 2,650 miles the trail officially covers (thanks to all our alternates and side quests), we were finally going to reach Canada! It was only 7 miles away. But after we reached the border, we’d have to begin the 30-mile backtrack to Harts Pass; sadly, walking into Canada is no longer allowed. So we set off at 7am as usual, planning to enjoy our time at the terminus, while hopefully still getting some good miles in this afternoon. As we left camp, a pika meeped at us. We took it as a blessing from the trail gods to continue.

The trail was a pretty gentle downhill for the first four miles. We alternated between comfortable silence and brief chats, pausing only once: to pretend to be bears in front of a wildlife camera. Then we arrived at a 3 mile section of blowdowns that had been much fearmongered on FarOut. We thought the rumours must have been overblown, but the deadfall turned out to be kind of gnarly. On the rest of the PCT the blowdowns have at least had their limbs sawed off, but these ones hadn’t been given that treatment and tough branches poked everywhere. I was trying to be careful not to scratch my legs again – I’d done enough of that in NorCal – but in the end I did manage to crack my patella into a branch, right over the top of an old scab from NorCal. It hurt pretty badly for a few seconds, but at least I’d look hardcore in our terminus photo.

We arrived at the top of a short series of switchbacks, and caught our first glimpse of a line of felled trees in the dense forest: that was the border. We could hear other people already at the terminus celebrating. This was it! Just as we finished the last switchback and were on the home stretch Sabretooth, who’d been in the lead, suddenly stopped. She started combing through her pack. We all realised why: we’d picked up a wooden clothespeg at Mazama and had been secretly hiding it in each others’ gear over the last few days. Whoever had it on them at the terminus would have to do a shoey. Out of someone else’s shoe. Satisfied that it wasn’t on her, Sabretooth picked up her bag and we charged towards the terminus, where we were greeted with cheers from the hikers already there.

The other hikers were already preparing to head out, so we wasted no time making them our photographers for group photos at the terminus. As well as a couple of videos of us first popping bubbles, and then doing shoeys. We did a play-by-play of the peg’s movements and discovered that it was with Catch. He took his punishment shoey well. It was only when the hustle and bustle finally died down that we took a seat and had time to take it in. It was a huge accomplishment, and yet it didn’t feel real. Or like the end. It did feel absolutely freezing. We were clearly in a katabatic zone – I’d been perfectly warm when we left camp this morning.

We spent about two hours there, enjoying each other’s company and that of a couple more hikers who arrived shortly after we did. But at the two hour mark the cold really started to get to us, and we prepared to leave. “Don’t you want to hear my speech?” Catch asked. I couldn’t believe I’d forgotten. We’d been badgering him for days to prepare a motivational speech for us. He climbed atop the terminus and we all looked up at him expectantly. Then he began to recite the lyrics to Miley Cyrus’s ‘The Climb’, with a couple of small changes to make it more appropriate: “It kinda was about how fast we got there / It kinda was about what’s waiting on the other side”.

We left in good spirits – the early morning alcohol probably helped with that – and began the climb back up to Hopkins Lake. We synched up playback of our hype playlist, which helped move us along. The pika meeped at us once again as we passed, which we took as a good sign. At the lake we paused for lunch, but not for long. The day had started with a beautiful blue sky, but had turned overcast, cold and windy.

It still didn’t feel quite real that we were done. Probably because we were still hiking. It was nice to have a few miles to walk and reflect and ease ourselves out of trail life. But we all agreed it would’ve been nice if this 30-mile section had been at least 10 miles shorter.

We crossed paths with hikers heading up to the terminus and made sure to fist bump them and cheer them on. Then we started running into familiar faces we hadn’t seen since NorCal, which was a nice surprise. But it meant that we arrived at the campsite we’d chosen in the dark, since we’d spent so much time chatting.

📍 Mile 2,625.2 | 🥾 22.85 km | ⛰️ +815m / -714m

There were only 11 miles between us and our final steps on the PCT. But rain was forecast, and we were keen to get out of it ASAP, so we set off at 7am as usual. The miles practically flew by as we chatted easily all morning, planning all the food we were going to eat now that trail was over. It drizzled lightly, on and off, and the clouds hung low around us so views were non-existent. We spotted a pair of hikers ahead of us and made it our mission to overtake them, which we finally accomplished just before we arrived at a trailhead. We decided to walk the road from there back to Harts Pass, since it would make for faster progress.

Just as we arrived at Harts and signed the last trail log, the rain really started to fall. We’d hoped the ranger would be in so we could call for a ride – there was no mobile service – but we were out of luck. There was only one car in the parking lot, and in this weather we didn’t hold too much hope for getting a hitch from it. So, since a note on the ranger’s door said there was service at a campsite a mile or so away, we decided to head there. It was better than sitting still and growing increasingly cold and wet in the rain.

Arriving at the campsite, though, none of us had any usable signal. Luckily, some day hikers there offered to let us use their phone; but we couldn’t get through to anyone. They said they could probably squeeze a couple of us in when they finished their hike, which we were very grateful for. We also had a lovely surprise, running into a group of hikers we knew well: in fact, it was Shakedown and Sabretooth’s earlier trail family. We spent a good while catching up, but standing still I grew increasingly cold, and eventually had to say goodbye so I could get moving to warm up.

Thankfully, Shakedown managed to convince some other people out for a day hike to allow us all to squeeze into their sedan. The driver turned out to be a volunteer SAR helicopter pilot, so we really lucked out. With three other people and a dog already in the car, though, it was a tight squeeze and we had to surrender our packs to the weather, strapping them to the roof racks. I shivered the whole way down the mountain, cold from the wind and rain. When the driver mentioned they’d been planning to stop at the Mazama Bakery for a coffee, we encouraged the break and gratefully paid for their coffees and ordered our own.

Not long afterwards we were being dropped at the doorstep of the Airbnb we’d booked in Winthrop, where we left our packs and went in search of food. And a celebratory beer, of course. Then we headed to the supermarket to grab some supplies for the next couple of days in town, before making ourselves at home in the Airbnb. Too lazy to cook, dinner was an easy spread of cheese and biscuits, as we cosied up in front of the fireplace to watch movies, introducing Shakedown to the delights of the Twilight franchise.

We slept in as long as our body clocks would allow, and then cooked a delicious big fry up for breakfast. It was a gorgeous, warm, blue-sky day outside, so I went for a bit of a wander around town to take advantage and keep my legs moving at least a little. When I got back we had a lunch of tomato soup and grilled cheese – which we’d fantasised about yesterday.

Then we began a room-to-room beer crawl, which we’d also dreamed up yesterday. Catch kicked us off with another motivational speech – this time, the Aussie classic, ‘Get on the Beers’ by Mashton Kutcher. In the end we only moved between the outdoor space at the front of the house, and the outdoor space at the back, since it was such a nice day it felt wrong to be inside. Slow and steady was definitely the name of the game, and we made it to dinnertime with plenty of beer to spare. As all good dinners should, we started with dessert: s’mores – my first ever, but certainly not my last. Dinner was some easy, delicious homemade pizzas, and we settled into the couch once more, to continue the Harry Potter marathon we’d started at White Pass.

This morning was much the same as yesterday morning – a relative sleep in, a fry up for breakfast – but the air was tinged with a little sadness. Today was our last day together as a group. When we’d finished breakfast and had packed up, reluctant to say goodbye just yet we headed down the main street to grab a coffee, chatting about which book would be our next book club pick, and trying to figure out where and when we could do a reunion hike.

At midday, though, it was time to go our separate ways. Shakedown and Sabretooth were heading to Vancouver, to continue their big year of travel. Catch was going with them, to catch a flight home for a family event. Sass and I were heading to Leavenworth, and then who knows where, as we passed a week waiting for Catch to meet us in Bend – the three of us were going back to fill in the miles we’d missed when we skipped around the smoke from the Austin fire. We hugged goodbye for now, and split in different directions.

Sass and I headed out of town and tried to hitch. Our backup plan was the bus, but it didn’t arrive for a couple of hours. We got lucky quickly: a pickup offered to take us to Twisp. We discovered that there was an earlier bus we could take from there, which connected conveniently with other buses all the way to Leavenworth. We decided to take it; neither of us had the energy to chat with hitches for a couple of hours. We wanted some time to be sad and morose about finishing the trail and saying goodbye to our friends.

The buses ran smoothly and we were dropped in Leavenworth in the late afternoon. There were lots of events on in town this weekend – including Oktoberfest, which was half the reason we’d come – so we made our way to the KOA in the hopes they’d still have a section for PCT hikers. We were in luck, and soon had our tents set up. Then we wandered into town to take advantage of the free beer Icicle Brewing offered to PCT hikers, and enjoyed people watching for a while before heading back to the campsite for an early night.

#8397. West Ridge or Hornbein Couloir? Everest Team Prepares for Fourth Attempt

The Russian team is preparing to head up Everest’s West Ridge for a fourth time. While no easy option exists, they want to avoid the extremely exposed, difficult, and uncertain ridge route. Their only alternative is the Hornbein Couloir, which would force them to stray temporarily into Tibet.

Andrei Vasiliev, Vitaly Shipilov, and Sergey Kondrashkin are in Kathmandu recovering from a viral infection and waiting out Cyclone Arnab, which is now weakening. They will return to their base in Lobuche this weekend, determined to climb Everest without supplemental oxygen.

Everest West Ridge some days ago. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

“So far, we have completed three rotations on the mountain,” leader Vasiliev told ExplorersWeb. “Part of this time was spent exploring different options for accessing the route.”

The Russian team has a permit to climb Everest from Nepal, as long as they attempt a route other than the standard Khumbu Icefall-South Col-Southeast Ridge. This has become the normal South Side route since Hillary and Tenzing’s first ascent in 1953.

Topo of the Russian team’s planned route on Everest, courtesy of Andrei Vasiliev

First, the Russians tried to bypass the Khumbu Icefall via the Nuptse Shoulder toward Camp 1, but heavy snow forced them to find another route. Crossing the Icefall (sharing paths with the normal route) was also too hard in the deep snow and on the shaky snow bridges over the innumerable crevasses.

“Eventually, we selected a third option, via the Lho La,” Vasiliev said. “From that pass, our planned route continues across the West Shoulder, along the West Ridge.”

At the Lho La col. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

On their latest foray, the team reached 6,400m. “We climbed approximately twelve 60m pitches over rock, snow, and ice of moderate difficulty,” said Vasiliev.

He noted that on the way to the West Shoulder, they found traces of previous expeditions, including old ropes and snow anchors.

As for the terrain ahead of them, Vasiliev said:

From our highest point reached, the terrain ahead looks manageable. We can see two more steep rock steps, each approximately 100m high, along with possible bypasses on steep snow slopes. Beyond these obstacles, the terrain appears easier, and we hope to be able to move simultaneously.

Rocky section on the way to Everest’s West Ridge. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Vasiliev and his team are confident they can manage this route, despite doing so in increasingly wintry conditions.

The route linking the Lho La, the West Shoulder, and the West Ridge of Everest has been completed only twice. A Yugoslavian team led by Tone Skarja did the first complete ascent in 1979. They used the Hornbein Couloir variation on their descent.

The only repetition was done by a Bulgarian team in 1984. Hristo Prodanov reached the summit on his own and retraced his steps down the ridge but never made it back alive. Some of his partners who summited days later descended via the normal route. Three other teams who climbed the West Shoulder-West Ridge summited by traversing to the North Face, on the Chinese side, and climbing the Hornbein Couloir.

The North Face of Everest from the West Shoulder. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev

Objectively speaking, the Hornbein Couloir offers more summit (and survival) chances than the upper part of the West Ridge. However, it requires traversing into Chinese territory. The Russian team has a permit to climb only from Nepal. It is unclear if a brief border trespass could be considered, and Vasiliev has not confirmed what they will do. “First we need to complete one more rotation,” he said.

#8390. Photo Contest Winners Reveal Amazing Microscopic Worlds

Since 1975, Nikon’s Small World competition has featured images produced by optical microscopes, an art that usually stays in scientific papers and textbooks. But through the carefully engineered lenses of the microscope, photomicrographers sometimes capture glimpses of strikingly surreal, alien beauty. The 2026 Photomicrography Competition winners include subjects both living and mechanical, small and very small.

The fruiting bodies of a Hemitrichia slime mold remind one distinctly of Dr. Seuss. Photo: Eric Epstein/Nikon Small World

The winning image shows bubbling globules of black ink being injected onto a piece of paper by an inkjet printer. Behind the lens was 25-year-old German design student Ole Bielfeldt, whose work explores the surprising complexity of everyday objects. His process is largely DIY: Bielfeldt builds his own setups, cobbles together parts, and learns techniques online.

“I just pick somewhere to start and go for it,” Bielfeldt explained. “You’re likely going to fail at first, and that’s what makes it even more interesting.”

The experimentation and imperfection, he added, are the most interesting parts of the process and, ultimately, more important to him than achieving the highest image quality.

Ah, mice; the humble martyrs to scientific progress. A significant amount of science seems to involve cutting up mice and learning from the result. But in this sort of photography, even the strongest mouse advocate must admit that the results are visually spectacular.

Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman of the University of Helsinki took this image of a mouse’s eye while researching drug therapy. Photo: Satu Paavonsalo and Dr. Sinem Karaman/Nikon Small World

Third place went to another rodent part: a 5X-magnified image of neurons in a mouse’s brain.

Photo: Kaelin Wulf and Rachel Flannery/Nikon Small World

In defense of humanity, we were also willing to subject our own body parts to photographic investigation. The 7th-place winner came from Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol at the Medical College of Georgia at Augusta University. Using confocal imaging, which involves scanning a specimen to generate optical sections, they captured human neurons at 20X magnification.

These human neurons were grown from reprogrammed skin cells. Photo: Dr. Bruno Cisterna and Dr. Eric Vitriol/Nikon Small World

I’ll end with a personal favorite of mine, John-Oliver Dum’s image of a little jumping spider, dusted with pollen. Dum, who won second place, credits a childhood bite for his fascination with spiders. The pollen was cultivated by his wife, specifically to create images like this one.

You can disagree, but I think this little guy is adorable. Photo: John-Oliver Dum

You can view the full gallery of winners and honorable mentions here. If you want to see photos of larger things, check out the winners from the Wildlife Photographer of the Year 2026, Aerial Photography, 2026 Ocean Photographer of the Year, or Memorial Maria Luisa International Photo and Video competitions.

#8387. Zero In Newton, NJ

I satisfy my cravings for town food and financial planning. I witness sports history.

What does a Trek blogger do with a free morning? The answer is…tax planning. Seriously. Personal finance is something of a hobby of mine. I had an idea while hiking during the week and wanted to model it and see the impact on my future tax liability. Riveting stuff, lemme tell ya.

While I had my nose buried in a spreadsheet I had one eye on the replay of yesterday’s F1 qualifying session for the Mexico City Grand Prix. Later in the day I could focus on the race itself which proved eventful. When the dust had settled, Formula One had its 2026 champion in Kimi Antonelli. Kimi stepped up in just his second season with a quixotic campaign to become the youngest ever Formula One champion. He is Italy’s first champion in 73 years. His championship is unquestionably well-deserved as he accumulated his large lead while dueling with 4 other F1 world champions, and shared this weekend’s podium with 2 of them in an incredible moment of serendipity. I won’t soon forget this season both for the unlikely champion and for having watched it while hiking the Appalachian Trail (and while writing this blog).

I celebrated Kimi’s title with unlimited soda refills, pizza, and ice cream, as is my usual M.O. The cafe gave me a peppermint mocha free of charge! I can’t say its something I’d order, I tend to stick to the basics with everything, including coffee, but I’ll admit it was pretty tasty.

I spent some time putting together a viable itinerary for the remainder of my hike. The plan gives me one day of buffer and an end date of November 22nd, assuming I take it easy over 3 days to complete the 4 state challenge during the southbound leg to be well rested to attempt to make the return trip northbound in a single day. Lately I’ve been wondering if I should record some video to document the attempt. It isn’t something I’ve done before, but this is certainly a year of firsts!

The Peppermint Mocha, tastes like the holidays.

Incredible. I now have less than 500 miles of hiking left to complete my journey. When I started out, I wasn’t sure it was possible. I had countless ideas to hike most of the trail by skipping sections if I didn’t feel up to the task. It doesn’t look like those will be necessary now.

It was a little bit of an up and down week. Tuesday felt like a new low after twisting my increasingly sensitive ankle several times. No worries though – its probably either a bruise or a slight stretch of the tendon. My ankles have survived years of hiking without feeling so much as a pinch. They are as strong as ever, just meeting their match on the slippery rocks this time of year.

Depending on where you draw the line, I officially completed New York either on Thursday or Saturday. The NY/NJ line I documented on Thursday is not the first time the trail enters New York heading northbound, it first enters New York shortly after the New Jersey high point, but soon crosses back into New Jersey and back again several times. I don’t think it is a coincidence that the AT follows the state line closely, it is likely the result of that stretch of land being public.

I also semi-retired my first pair of Altra Olympus 6 shoes that I put on at the start of the White Mountains since they have now accumulated 1,000 miles. They seem to have plenty of life left, they will accrue more miles on future hikes for sure.

Welcome to November, its finishing month! The time change will be welcome, I feel lazy waiting for the sun to come up to start hiking only to realize that it is already 8:00AM by the time I actually make it onto the trail. The time change won’t bring any more daylight, it will be startling to see daylight running out before 5:00PM.

My first 2-day stint will see me finish all but about 1 mile of New Jersey. I’ll be crossing the Delaware Water Gap on Wednesday and setting foot in Pennsylvania for the first time since mid-July. There are warmer days ahead, but also a chance of rain later in the week. Rocks are guaranteed, northern Pennsylvania is infamous for them. We’ll see if their reputation is warranted.

#8385. College Students Found Dead After Hiking Colorado Mountain

The two young men who set off into Colorado’s Sawatch Mountains this month were both passionate about taking the outdoors seriously. One was studying to be a wildland firefighter, while the other hoped to become a mountain guide.

But both of them were found dead Wednesday, under circumstances that remain unclear. Local authorities spent days looking for missing hikers Kaden Matsuda, 19, and Jackson Donlon, 20.

The bodies were finally discovered near West Apostle Mountain on October 28, just outside of Gunnison, Colorado.

Matsuda and Donlon, students at Colorado Mountain College in Leadville, had planned on hiking and camping near Ice Mountain, a 13,960-foot peak located about 50 miles from Gunnison.

They left for their trip on Oct. 23. College staff notified local authorities they were missing on Oct. 26, according to the Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office. The men’s families said they were both experienced hikers.

Matsuda was studying to be a wildland firefighter, and Donlon was training to become a mountain guide.

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Kaden Matsuda, left, and Jackson Donlon. Supplied: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Search-and-rescue teams were deployed and found their vehicle at the trailhead. Weather conditions looked risky, with heavy snow falling in Chaffee County.

“Ice Mountain is a very technical climb, and it is recommended that hikers be very experienced when trying to tackle it. That is when it is dry. Although there was only about eight inches of snow around Kaden’s vehicle and in the lower basin, Ice Mountain received one to two feet of snow,” the sheriff’s office said in a Facebook post.

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Multiple local SAR teams worked on the case. Photo: Chaffee County Sheriff’s Office

Rescue teams used drones, helicopters, and dogs to search for the two hikers. On October 27, they located their tent, which had collapsed under the weight of the snow, near West Apostle Mountain (13,597 feet). Inside were sleeping bags, stoves, and other equipment, but the two men were nowhere to be found.

The next day, authorities announced they had found their bodies in the mountain’s basin. Officials declined to share potential causes of death, beyond stating that they did not suspect foul play.

The Sawatch Range of the Rocky Mountains is home to many 13,000- and 14,000-foot peaks. Some of them, like West Apostle Mountain, require technical climbing ability and become substantially more difficult and dangerous during wet weather. The route up the mountain requires traversing fields of loose boulder scree and talus that can be hazardous after snow.

From 2010 to 2017, eight people have died in the Sawatch Mountains. Falls are the most common cause of fatalities for those tackling Colorado’s 13ers and 14ers, as the state’s highest mountains are known to locals.

#8379. Rock Spire Collapses at Popular Turkish Tourist Site, Killing Three

Part of a rock spire known as a fairy chimney collapsed yesterday near the entrance to one of Turkey’s most popular tourist destinations, killing three people and injuring five others.

The incident occurred around 3:15 pm local time in the town of Goreme, in central Turkey’s Cappadocia region yesterday. Rocks broke away and fell onto people near the parking area. The site is part of a UNESCO World Heritage landscape, famous for its cave dwellings and cone-shaped rock formations. Nevsehir Governor Huseyin Kok said that heavy rainfall triggered a landslide that caused the rocks to detach from the formation, according to Reuters.

Rescue teams initially recovered two bodies from the rubble before discovering a third victim overnight, bringing the death toll to three. The deceased include two Turkish citizens and one foreign national. Five others were injured in the collapse. Some of them were later discharged from hospital, according to AFP.

Eyewitnesses described a loud noise followed by a large dust cloud. The area was closed to the public, and search operations concluded overnight under floodlights.

Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek said an investigation by the chief prosecutor’s office, along with expert assessments, would begin. The collapse occurred on Turkey’s Republic Day, a public holiday when visitor numbers were high.

Cappadocia, in central Anatolia, is renowned for its distinctive fairy chimneys. These tall, thin spires of soft volcanic rock topped by harder caps were shaped over millions of years by wind and water erosion. The Goreme Open-Air Museum and surrounding sites were put on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1985 for their blend of natural landforms and human history, including Byzantine rock-cut churches and underground settlements. The region’s soft rock is geologically fragile and prone to weathering and occasional rockfalls, particularly after heavy rain.

Turkish authorities have previously carried out restoration and monitoring work to address erosion and climate-related risks, and smaller non-fatal collapses were recorded in the area in 2024 and 2025. The site remains one of Turkey’s most visited destinations, drawing tourists for hot-air balloon rides, hiking, and exploration of its unique geology and heritage.
